docs.title: Impact Model
docs.text:
Impact Model is an AI-native format from ProductBuildersHQ for describing how a program, product, or organization expects to bring about change. It is a causal model: it states which interventions should change which outcomes, why each step should lead to the next, and how to measure whether it did. It is a Go-first data model with generated JSON Schema, plus an SDK, the impact-model CLI, and an MCP server.

You describe the change once, in one impact model. The theory of change, the logic model, the outcome map, the logframe, strategy formats such as OKRs and V2MOM, and improvement formats such as DMAIC are projections of it. Each draws the same model for a different reader and leaves something out, and none of them is a part of another.

flowchart LR
  classDef model fill:#fff4cc,stroke:#b8860b,stroke-width:2px,color:#111
  classDef method fill:#eef7ee,stroke:#2e7d32,color:#111
  classDef strategy fill:#e8eefc,stroke:#3f51b5,color:#111
  classDef planned fill:#f3f3f3,stroke:#757575,stroke-dasharray:4 3,color:#111

  im["Impact model<br/>outcomes, causal links, assumptions, evidence,<br/>interventions, indicators, audiences"]:::model
  im --> toc["Theory of change"]:::method
  im --> lm["Logic model"]:::method
  im --> om["Outcome map"]:::method
  im --> lf["Logframe"]:::method

  im --> v2["V2MOM"]:::strategy
  im --> dm["DMAIC"]:::strategy

docs.title: What is an impact model?
docs.text:
An impact model is one structured description of how and why change is expected to happen. It holds:

  • the outcomes that should change, at five levels from output to impact, and the causal links between them, each with a reason to believe it;
  • the assumptions that must hold for a link to work, and the evidence for and against them;
  • what is done to bring the change about: interventions, and the resources and outputs they need and produce;
  • how progress is measured: indicators, targets, and observations over time;
  • who is accountable for each change, and who needs to see what.

Every element records where it came from (stated, inferred, a hypothesis, or confirmed), so a reader can tell what an organization has claimed from what an assistant has proposed.

The model is a graph of causes and measures. A diagram or a table of it is a projection, and one model can produce many.

docs.title: Projections
docs.text:
Each projection answers a different question for a different reader:

Projection Answers Get it with Problem tree What is the problem, what causes it, and what does it lead to? The core problem in the middle, causes (roots) below and effects (branches) above, with the outcomes that address each. See the guide report problem-tree, problem-tree-d2, problem-tree-json Theory of change Why should what we do lead to the change we want, and in what order must outcomes happen? Drawn as pathways of change, from the earliest outcome at the bottom to the long-term goal at the top report pathway Outcome map What changes, who is responsible for each change, and how is it measured? The outcomes by level, each with its sphere, owner, cause, and indicators report outcome-map Logic model What goes in, what is done, and what comes out? Stages from inputs, activities, and outputs through short-, medium-, and long-term outcomes to impact, one per pathway report logic-model, logic-model-d2 Logframe What do we promise, and how will we verify it? Narrative, indicators with targets, means of verification, and assumptions, for contracts and monitoring report logframe Metric tree and headline metrics What does each program steer by, and what is each audience told? report metric-tree, report headline OKRs and outcome journeys What will a team commit to this quarter, and how does a person move through the outcomes? For the PRISM planning tools export okr, export journey V2MOM What do we want, what matters, how will we get it, what is in the way, and how will we know? Vision and values from the context, one method per pathway with its interventions as projects, measures from each pathway's North Star and guardrails, and obstacles from risks and open assumptions. See the mapping export v2mom DMAIC Which metrics are we improving, from what baseline to what target, what causes the gap, and is the gain holding? One category per pathway marked projections: [dmaic], its numeric indicators as metrics with observations as data points, control limits once there are enough, root causes from the problem tree, and interventions as improvement initiatives. Lint first checks that those pathways are measured often enough. See the mapping export dmaic

Each projection leaves something out. A logic model shows the sequence from what goes in to what comes out, and rarely why each step holds. A theory of change shows why, and says less about what is delivered. A logframe fits the model into a matrix for contracts, and OKRs keep only what a team commits to for a period. None is derived from another. The impact model holds what they all need, so any of them can be drawn from it. A logic model that arrives on its own can seed a candidate impact model, but it cannot supply the reasons and assumptions it never held, so those stay marked as inferred until someone confirms them.

impact-model report pathway impact-model.yaml           # the theory of change, as pathways of change
impact-model report outcome-map impact-model.yaml       # the outcome map
impact-model report logic-model impact-model.yaml       # a logic model for each pathway
impact-model report logframe impact-model.yaml          # the logframe matrix
impact-model report definitions impact-model.yaml       # all of them, plus metrics and glossary
impact-model export okr impact-model.yaml               # OKRs for the PRISM tools

Change the model once and every projection changes with it, so the numbers and labels never drift apart. (The outcome map here is the outcomes framework from the ActKnowledge method; it is not IDRC's Outcome Mapping, which tracks progress markers for the partners a program influences.)

docs.title: The theory of change
docs.text:
The theory of change is the projection most programs start from. It explains how and why a program expects to bring about a change. It starts from the long-term goal and works backwards: what conditions must exist for the goal to be reached, what must exist before each of those, and so on down to what the program does today. Each step is an outcome; each arrow between outcomes is a causal link with a reason for believing it holds; and each belief that has to be true for a link to work is an assumption that can be tested.

flowchart BT
    A[Staff write strong applications] -->|skilled staff apply more often| C[Members win more funding]
    B[Members share a funder list] -->|shared leads widen the pool| C
    C -->|funded work reaches more residents| D[Residents are better served]
    classDef ceiling stroke-dasharray: 4 3
    class D ceiling

An illustration only. The dashed outcome sits above the organization's ceiling of accountability: the program tracks it and contributes to it, but does not claim it.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
The method is used by foundations, development agencies, and funders, and the sources agree on five reasons:

  • Planning. Agree on what has to change, and in what order, before spending money on activities.
  • Closing the "missing middle". Show how day-to-day activities connect to a long-term goal, instead of asserting that they do.
  • Evaluability. Indicators and tests come from the causal reasoning, so you know what to measure and what would count as being wrong.
  • Communication. Funders, partners, staff, and the people the program serves can see the same reasoning and argue with it.
  • Learning. The model is a living framework. When evidence arrives, you revise it instead of defending it.

docs.title: How the chain, the metrics, and what each audience sees fit together
docs.text:
An impact model is the chain from resources to impact. Metrics hang off each step of it, and different readers should see a different few. The first diagram is one program, shown as a pathway. The second shows how its metrics reach each audience.

flowchart LR
  classDef step fill:#eef7ee,stroke:#2e7d32,color:#111
  classDef metric fill:#e8eefc,stroke:#3f51b5,color:#111
  classDef focus fill:#fff4cc,stroke:#b8860b,stroke-width:2px,color:#111
  classDef above fill:#f3f3f3,stroke:#757575,color:#111

  subgraph program["One program, shown as a pathway. Every arrow carries a reason, assumptions, and evidence"]
    res["Resources<br/>inputs"]:::step --> act["Activities<br/>interventions"]:::step
    act --> outp["Outputs"]:::step
    outp --> st["Short-term<br/>outcomes"]:::step
    st --> mid["Medium-term<br/>outcomes"]:::step
    mid --> lt["Long-term<br/>outcomes"]:::step
  end
  subgraph above["Above the ceiling of accountability: tracked, not owned"]
    imp["Impact"]:::above
  end
  lt -.->|contribution| imp

  m1["Input and activity metrics<br/>staff hours, events held"]:::metric
  m2["Output metrics<br/>reach, attendee hours"]:::metric
  m3["Outcome metrics, the drivers<br/>skills gained, practice applied"]:::metric
  ns["North Star<br/>one per program"]:::focus
  gr["Guardrails<br/>equity, quality, burden"]:::focus
  mi["Impact metric<br/>reported as a contribution"]:::metric

  res -.-> m1
  act -.-> m1
  outp -.-> m2
  st -.-> m3
  mid -.-> m3
  lt -.-> ns
  ns -.- gr
  imp -.-> mi

Reading the first diagram:

  • Resource and activity metrics show what went in and what was done. Output metrics show reach. Outcome metrics are the drivers: they say whether the change the program is for is happening.
  • A North Star is the one number that best captures the value a program delivers to the people it serves. It sits on the highest outcome the program answers for, at or below the ceiling of accountability, and it is an outcome, never a count of outputs. Each program can have its own, because programs deliver different value. Guardrails keep it honest by watching what it could hurt, such as equity, quality, or staff burden.
  • Impact sits above the ceiling. It is tracked and contributed to, not claimed.
flowchart LR
  classDef metric fill:#e8eefc,stroke:#3f51b5,color:#111
  classDef focus fill:#fff4cc,stroke:#b8860b,stroke-width:2px,color:#111
  classDef out fill:#eef7ee,stroke:#2e7d32,color:#111

  subgraph lib["One metric library: every number is defined once"]
    common["Common-layer metrics<br/>same definition in every program"]:::metric
    drivers["Output, driver, and activity metrics"]:::metric
    ns["North Star for each program"]:::focus
    gr["Guardrails"]:::focus
  end

  assigned["Indicators assigned to each audience"]:::metric
  lib --> assigned

  subgraph head["Headline metrics: a short, ordered list per audience, worded for that audience"]
    hb["Board and leadership"]:::focus
    hf["Funders"]:::focus
    hm["Members"]:::focus
    hg["Government"]:::focus
    hc["Community"]:::focus
  end
  assigned --> head

  subgraph channels["Where each audience sees them"]
    cb["Board deck, quarterly review"]:::out
    cf["Funder summary, grant report"]:::out
    cm["Newsletter, member survey results"]:::out
    cg["Policy briefings"]:::out
    cc["Annual impact report, website"]:::out
  end
  hb --> cb
  hf --> cf
  hm --> cm
  hg --> cg
  hc --> cc
  hf --> cc
  hb --> cc

Reading the second diagram:

  • Every number is defined once, in one metric library. Two audiences that see the same figure see the same figure, with the same caveats and the same marker for whether it is attributable to the work or a contribution.
  • Headline metrics are what you tell people. The North Star is what you steer by. They can differ. The board, funders, members, government, and the community each get a short list, worded for them, drawn from the same indicators. A North Star may lead one list and not appear in another.
  • Every box is something you can record and report today. Mark an indicator as a program's North Star, with its guardrails, in the pathway's focus. Give each audience an ordered, worded headline list. impact-model report metric-tree shows a program's North Star and every indicator from activity to impact, and impact-model report headline shows what each audience is told. The amber boxes are the choices you make: which number a program steers by, and which few each audience leads with. impact-model lint checks them.

docs.title: What this project gives you
docs.text:
Benefit How A model you can trust Every element records whether a source stated it, you inferred it, it is still a hypothesis, or reviewers confirmed it. Reports show how much of the model is established and how much is our reading Edits that cannot make it worse One validated, atomic patch engine behind the CLI, the SDK, and the AI tools. A change that adds structural errors is rejected, and --dry-run shows the result first Quality you can check A schema, structural validation, 72 deterministic lint rules, and a rubric for human or AI judges, so "is this a good impact model?" has an answer you can repeat Progress you can measure Load a spreadsheet of numbers and see which indicators, outcomes, and pathways are on track, with assumptions that can cap a result and a confidence score for each route to impact Artifacts for each audience Executive and funder reports, audience stories, slide decks, Word and PowerPoint files, CSV tables, and OKR exports, all from one source and stamped with the version and hash Review that comes back Send a packet or sheet to reviewers, import their answers as proposed changes you inspect, then record approval Honest handling of people's data Stories and quotes appear only with consent, and restricted evidence is never rendered anywhere Ready for AI agents An MCP server with ten tools and five skills lets an agent draft, edit, measure, and report, under the same rules as a person

It is meant for program and strategy teams, evaluators, funders, and anyone who has to explain why what they do should lead to what they hope for, and then show whether it did.

docs.title: Concepts → Go Types
docs.text:
How each concept from the research brief (§8 entity model, §9.8 UNDG implications) maps to the Go model in pkg/impact. The TRD §7 is normative; this page is the index.

The model is one impact model. The methods the research brief describes are projections of it, drawn by the report command:

Method Projection shows Report kinds Problem tree The core problem, its causes (roots) below and its effects (branches) above, with the outcomes that address each problem-tree, problem-tree-d2, problem-tree-json Theory of change Pathways of change, with the reasons and assumptions behind each link pathway Logic model Inputs, activities, outputs, and outcomes by level, for each pathway logic-model, logic-model-layered, logic-model-d2 Outcome map Outcomes by level, with who is responsible for each outcome-map Logframe A matrix of narrative, indicators, verification, and assumptions logframe

OKRs and outcome journeys are projections too, written by export okr and export journey for the PRISM planning tools, and so is a V2MOM, written by export v2mom (see the V2MOM guide), and a DMAIC metrics document for pathways marked projections: [dmaic], written by export dmaic (see the DMAIC guide).

Delivered by names the roadmap item (RMI-THEORYOFCHANGESPEC-NNN, shown as NNN) that adds the type or field. Concepts not in v0 are listed under Deferred.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Term Meaning in this specification Impact The highest-level change, usually above the ceiling of accountability; contribution is claimed, not achievement Long-term outcome The goal the initiative holds itself accountable for Outcome A condition that must exist for the theory to work and does not yet exist, phrased as a state, not an activity Output A direct product of an intervention, within the organization's control Core problem The problem the impact model responds to, context.problemStatement; the middle of the problem tree Cause A condition that leads to the core problem, directly or through other causes; a root of the problem tree Effect A consequence of the core problem, directly or through other effects; a branch of the problem tree Precondition An outcome that must hold for a higher outcome; incoming links to an outcome are its preconditions Precondition group An explicit AND / OR / k-of-n combination of preconditions Causal link A directed claim that one outcome (or intervention) contributes to another, with a rationale Intervention Something the actors do to bring about outcomes (program, product, policy, advocacy, partnership…). The logic model shows interventions as activities, and the V2MOM projection shows them as a method's projects. An initiative is the organizational effort that delivers one, linked through initiativeRefs Assumption A condition believed to hold for a link or outcome to work, which the initiative does not bring about Indicator Measurable evidence that an outcome, output, or assumption is changing Ceiling of accountability The line above which outcomes are tracked but not owned Pathway A named grouping of outcomes, interventions, and indicators, such as a program area Provenance basis Whether an element was stated by a source, inferred, proposed as a hypothesis, confirmed, or rejected in review Observation set A separate document of measured values, assumption assessments, stories, and learning reviews for a period

docs.title: Credits
docs.text: This specification stands on a long body of work on Theory of Change and on evaluation. Where it takes an idea, a term, or a structure from that work, the source is named here. The research brief is the full record: it summarizes each source and gives the citations.

Casey Foundation (Reisman and Gienapp, 2004) Outcomes arranged along time horizons Outcome levels and lag Aspen Institute Roundtable on Community Change (Weiss, 1995; Anderson, 2005) Theory-driven evaluation, and the three quality criteria of plausible, feasible, and testable qualityReview on revisions and the review rubric Outcome Mapping (Earl, Carden, and Smutylo, IDRC, 2001) Spheres of control, influence, and interest, and boundary partners Outcome.sphere, the boundary_partner actor role Contribution analysis (Mayne) Separating a claim of attribution from a claim of contribution Indicator.claim, and the lint rule that indicators above the ceiling claim contribution Process tracing (Van Evera, 1997; combined with contribution analysis by Befani and Mayne, 2014) Grading evidence for a causal link with the straw-in-the-wind, hoop, smoking-gun, and doubly decisive tests Evidence.processTracingTest Most Significant Change (Davies and Dart, 2005) Stories of change coded into themes so they can be counted Stories, themes, and the story codebook Outcome Harvesting (Wilson-Grau and Britt, 2012) Outcomes found after the fact, as a kind of evidence The outcome_harvest evidence type The logic model and logical framework traditions (W.K. Kellogg Foundation, 2004; USAID; UNDG, Results-Based Management Handbook, 2011) The linear views of a theory The logic-model and logframe reports

Isabel Vogel's review of how Theory of Change is used in international development (DFID, 2012) makes the point, quoted in the research brief, that a logic model without reference to its context is closer to a logframe than to a theory of change. In that spirit this spec keeps assumptions, risks, and context in the same document as the pathways.

docs.title: Projects and software
docs.text:
This project is part of the PRISM family of projects by the same author. It uses prism-core for shared types, structured-goals for OKR types, prism-roadmap as the target of the OKR and outcome-journey exports, and structured-evaluation for rubrics and GO and NO-GO reports. Operating-system differences are handled by oscompat.

The command line is built on Cobra and pflag, YAML is read and written with yaml.v3, documents are checked with santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema, the schemas are generated from the Go types with invopop/jsonschema, and the MCP server uses the official Go SDK. The list of every module compiled into the binary, with its license and copyright notice, is in THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md.

Some commands call Marp, the Mermaid CLI, and Pandoc when they are installed. They are not included. This site is built with MkDocs and the Material theme, and its page template comes from visionspec.

docs.title: How the sources are used
docs.text:
• The definitions, guidance, and examples in this documentation are written in our own words. The research brief quotes sources in short passages, each attributed to its author.
  • All examples are fictional: the organizations, people, numbers, and URLs are invented. No example describes a real organization.
  • The names of organizations and publications are used to credit their work. Naming a source does not mean that its authors or publishers have reviewed or endorse this project.
  • This project is licensed under the MIT License. The software it depends on keeps its own licenses, which are all permissive.

If a credit is missing or wrong, please open an issue.

docs.title: Model feedback from authoring the reference examples
docs.text:
Two fictional reference impact models (examples/intermediary and examples/market-adoption) were written against the model to find what it could not say, or said awkwardly. This page records each finding and what was decided, so the reasoning outlives the conversation that produced it.

Decisions are done (implemented and tested), documented (a convention, now written down), planned (assigned to a roadmap item), or declined (with the reason).

docs.title: Done
docs.text: Finding Decision A network-wide roll-up or common-layer indicator has no single outcome to measure, so it was attached to an arbitrary one An indicator's measures may name a pathway. Validation accepts it, and a pathway-filtered view includes pathway-level indicators only for that pathway Ordinal levels cannot be summed or averaged, so a "median level" lived only in formula text Added median and mode aggregations No actor type for a government office; no external-factor kind for an opportunity (risks already had one) Added the government actor type and the opportunity factor kind What may a restricted evidence record contain, and what do renderers show? A restricted record (or one with no sensitivity set) may carry a title, type, strength, and source. Its excerpt, summary, and URL are withheld by every renderer, since a URL can reveal where a confidential document lives A group's target is one outcome; nothing said what a nested group's target is A nested group targets the same outcome as the group containing it. Validation enforces it (VAL-GRP-004) The coverage rule wanted an indicator on every owned outcome, which inflates indicator counts IMP-MEA-001 accepts coverage through another indicator's proxyFor

docs.title: Documented
docs.text: Finding Decision direction: increase is vague for a qualitative indicator whose rise is bad news direction states the desired direction. If a rising level is bad news, the direction is decrease; say why in the indicator's definition Negative-polarity links and precondition logic A negative link is an inhibitor, not a precondition: it does not count toward all, any, or at_least logic or toward k. How an inhibitor lowers a pathway's status is decided with the roll-up algorithm (RMI-THEORYOFCHANGESPEC-018) A competitor's momentum has no element type Model it as an outcome in the interest sphere with category respond, linked to the outcomes it inhibits. A first-class competitor-response element is deferred until a second example needs it Capability relation dependsOn is camelCase while every other enum is snake_case It comes from prism-core's shared CapabilityRef and is intentionally left alone so the PRISM modules stay interchangeable In YAML flow mappings ({a: b, c: d}), an unquoted comma inside a value silently splits the mapping Schema validation catches it. The authoring guide recommends block style, which fmt always produces provenance.decidedBy is free text, so nothing stops a personal name By convention it names a group or role. Detecting personal names is not something code can do reliably; the authoring guide and the review checklist say so Responsibility (own, shared, partner) and a problem tree are not modelled Both are in RMI-THEORYOFCHANGESPEC-044. Until then the ceiling is a level and root causes are text

docs.title: Planned
docs.text: Finding Roadmap item A weighted_mean roll-up cannot be computed if the weight metric has no indicator Lint rule IMP-MET-003, in RMI-THEORYOFCHANGESPEC-014 pathway.outcomeIds and indicators' pathwayIds are two lists kept consistent by hand Lint rule IMP-PTH-003, in RMI-THEORYOFCHANGESPEC-014 A group's members should each have a link into the group's target Already covered by IMP-STR-007, in RMI-THEORYOFCHANGESPEC-013 Assumption appliesTo and a link's assumptionIds can disagree A consistency lint rule, in RMI-THEORYOFCHANGESPEC-014

docs.title: Declined (for now)
docs.text: Finding Reason A window field on metrics ("trailing twelve months") Useful, but it changes how observations and targets are compared, so it deserves its own design. It is recorded for a later minor version; until then the window is stated in the formula One indicator measuring both an outcome and an assumption Two indicators are clearer and cost little. Revisit if authors keep hitting it A "key outcome" or "monitored" flag on outcomes proxyFor already expresses "this indicator also stands in for that outcome" without a second mechanism A layer label on outcomes for two-layer impact Layer one versus layer two is already visible through sphere, the indicator claim, and the ceiling of accountability. A fourth signal would add overlap, not information changeType has no standardization That value describes what an intervention does, not the kind of change an outcome describes; the outcome's adoption or policy change type fits

docs.title: ADR 0001: Rename the project to impact-model
docs.text: Status: Accepted Date: 2026-11-01

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The project began as a specification for a Theory of Change, and was named theoryofchange-spec. It now holds more than that. One document records the outcomes and causal links of a program, the assumptions and evidence behind them, the interventions that bring them about, how progress is measured, who needs to see which numbers, and where each claim came from. The same document is drawn as a theory of change, a logic model, an outcome map, and a logframe, and it exports to OKRs.

Two things made the name wrong:

  • Scope. The name says the document is a Theory of Change, and the other methods look like parts of it or exports from it. A logic model is not a part of a theory of change. It is a more operational projection of the same underlying thing, and each projection leaves out what another keeps.
  • Direction. The project is aimed at more than nonprofits. A product team has the same need to say why an intervention should move a metric, and to keep what it believes apart from what it has observed.

The published releases, v0.1.0 and v0.2.0, had no known users, so renaming cost little.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
The project is the impact model. The theory of change, the logic model, the pathway of change, the outcome map, and the logframe are projections of it, and so are strategy formats: OKRs, which the model already exports, and V2MOM, which is among the follow-ups. "Projection" names a method's rendering of the model. It is not report.View, the data a report is built from.

Was Is github.com/ProductBuildersHQ/theoryofchange-spec github.com/ProductBuildersHQ/impact-model command theoryofchange command impact-model packages pkg/toc, pkg/tocio pkg/impact, pkg/impactio type toc.Document impact.Model kind: TheoryOfChange, TheoryOfChangeStatus kind: ImpactModel, ImpactModelStatus schemas theory-of-change, theory-of-change-status impact-model, impact-model-status theory.yaml impact-model.yaml fields tocId, childToc modelId, childModel cross-document reference toc:<id>#<element> model:<id>#<element> lint rule IDs TOC-STR-001 IMP-STR-001 flag --toc flag --model MCP tools toc_*, skills toc-* impact_*, impact-*

docs.title: What did not change
docs.text:
• The method names. report pathway, logic-model, outcome-map, and logframe are still the names of those projections, and the research brief still describes the Theory of Change method.
  • specVersion, which stays 0.1. The reader accepts any 0.x.
  • Identifiers of the work. The initiative INIT-THEORYOFCHANGESPEC-001 and the roadmap items RMI-THEORYOFCHANGESPEC-* keep their names, since an identifier is not a label. New roadmap items take the repository's new slug, RMI-IMPACTMODEL-001 onward, so the two series sit side by side in one initiative.
  • The quality rubric and the specification template in spec/. They are the theory of change quality checklist and outline, and will become the rubric of that projection.
  • The example's own title. The membership network example is a theory of change, and says so.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Releases. v0.1.0 and v0.2.0 were published under the old module path and stay there. A module cannot change its path under an existing tag, so the first release under the new name is v0.3.0.
  • Migration. A document written for v0.2.0 needs kind: ImpactModel, the renamed fields, and level: medium_term if it predates that change. Nothing else in the format moves.
  • Links. GitHub redirects the old repository address. The documentation site moves to a new path.
  • No alias. The old command name is not kept, since nobody uses it.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
Name Why not Keep theoryofchange-spec Understates the scope and ranks the other methods below one of them impact-model-spec Matches the naming of some sibling repositories, but this repository also ships a command, an SDK, and an MCP server structured-impact-model Longer, and "structured" adds nothing a schema does not already say impact-spec Broad enough to mean almost anything

impact-model has one real drawback: the phrase also means financial and environmental impact assessment. The tagline says what it is, and "impact" is already the name of the top outcome level.

A leadership framework with a similar name exists in another project. The two are unrelated and independent, and nothing here depends on it.

docs.title: Follow-ups, not decided here
docs.text:
• A theory-of-change report kind, so each method is a named projection.
  • context.values, and an export to V2MOM beside the existing export to OKRs, with the OKR and V2MOM documents staying separate and linked to the model by ID.
  • A report saying which projections a given model has enough information to draw.
  • Relations between indicators, such as one predicting another, with the evidence for each.

docs.title: Rubric discrimination evaluation
docs.text: Does the core rubric tell a sound theory from a weak one, and do two independent judges agree? Two judges scored two theories against the core rubric (12 categories) through impact-model judge.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
• Reference theory: examples/intermediary/impact-model.yaml, after it was extended with measurement design and change analysis. Lint: GO under the standard profile, 0 errors, 9 warnings.
  • Weak theory: docs/evals/fixtures/weak-impact-model.yaml, a fictional theory seeded with the usual faults: a vague problem, outcomes that restate activities, no rationale or assumption on its one causal link, no evidence, no consultation, one unexplained indicator. It validates; lint is GO with 6 warnings.
  • Judges: two Claude models run as separate sub-agents from one Claude Code session, each with only the bundle and a skeleton to fill in, and told not to read anything else. Judge names in the verdict files are sonnet and haiku.
  • Procedure: judge show built a bundle per theory; each judge returned a verdict naming the bundle hash; judge record checked and stored it; judge summary combined them (majority; a tie goes to partial).

Verdicts and summaries are in docs/evals/verdicts/: run1/ holds the first run of both theories, run2/ the second run of the reference theory after it was improved (below).

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Reference theory Weak theory Categories failed (sonnet / haiku) 0 / 0 9 / 8 Categories partial (sonnet / haiku) 5 / 5 3 / 4 Categories passed (sonnet / haiku) 7 / 7 0 / 0 Exact agreement on category scores 83% (10 of 12) 92% (11 of 12) High-severity findings, consolidated 0 13 Passes the rubric No No
  • Discrimination holds. The weak theory fails 8 or 9 categories under each judge; the reference fails none. The rubric's requirement that a weak theory fail at least 3 categories is met by a wide margin.
  • Agreement is good where it matters. The judges differ on two categories for the reference (evidence, plausible) and one for the weak theory (plausible), each by one step (pass against partial, or partial against fail), never across the pass-fail gap.
  • The reference theory does not pass. Both judges scored five required categories partial: process (residents, the least-heard group, and county officials are not consulted), targeting (outcomes name target groups but few indicators break results down by them), testable, and structural_integrity (the nine lint warnings, which the rubric reads as "not clean"), plus evidence or plausible depending on the judge. The rubric needs every required category to pass and allows three medium findings; the judges raised seven.

docs.title: Second run: after improving the example
docs.text:
The first run named concrete gaps in the reference theory, and they were fixed: residents and county staff were consulted (two new consultation records), the two high-stakes assumptions without evidence now cite it, the indicator for the low-access residents is broken down by that group, four indicators gained baselines and targets, the retention rate gained the weight it needed, and the assessment report now counts indicators that stand in for an outcome. The example lints with 0 errors and 0 warnings under the standard profile. The two judges then scored the new bundle.

Reference theory Sonnet Haiku Combined (majority) Pass / partial / fail 10 / 2 / 0 6 / 6 / 0 6 / 6 / 0 Decision conditional conditional does not pass
  • Every category that was partial for process, targeting, testable, and structural integrity in run 1 improved: Sonnet now passes all four, Haiku passes two. No category fails under either judge.
  • The remaining partials are different ones: Sonnet scores evidence and plausible partial; Haiku scores logic_flow, assumptions_risks, targeting, plausible, feasible, and testable partial, with new findings (combination logic at two outcomes, two long-term outcomes measured only by candidate indicators, an assumption test that cites a retired indicator).
  • Exact agreement fell to 50%, from 83% in run 1. The stricter judge (Haiku) raised new, mostly medium, findings each time; the gap between the two judges is now larger than the gap between the example and a pass.
  • plausible is partial under both judges, for a reason that is true: an eight-person network running three pathways, with resident-level change expected within three years.

Under the rule "every required category passes", the reference theory does not pass in either run. Under a rule of "no failed category and no high findings", it passes in both, and both judges call it conditional.

docs.title: Acceptance
docs.text: The bar for sending the reference example to human review is that no judge raises a high or critical finding on it. Both runs meet it: run 1 raised no high or critical findings under either judge, and neither did run 2. The rubric's own pass rule (every required category passes, at most three medium findings) stays as it is; it is the bar for approving a theory, not for sharing an example for review.

docs.title: What this means
docs.text:
The rubric separates the two theories clearly and the judges agree closely enough to trust it. The stated acceptance, that the reference example passes, is not met as written, and the cause is the example and the pass rule, not a disagreement between judges:

  • The example had real gaps that both judges named independently in run 1. They have been closed. A second run shows the example is better, but not that it can be made to pass: a judge asked to find what is missing finds something each time.
  • The pass rule, "every required category passes", is strict for a worked example. A theory with no failed category and no high findings is judged conditional, which is a defensible reading of "sound enough to show".

docs.title: Limits
docs.text: Two judges, two theories, one run each for the weak theory and two for the reference. The judges are not independent of the people who wrote the rubric and fixtures. The weak theory is deliberately weak, so this shows the rubric is not blind, not that it grades subtle cases well. Verdict shape: one judge returned fields in a slightly different shape and its file was reshaped to the skeleton (category key, metadata) before recording; no score, reasoning, or finding was changed.

docs.title: User Guides
docs.text:
These guides take you from a first impact model to reports, review, and an AI agent working on the same file. Each one stands alone; read them in this order if you are new.

  1. Getting started: install, create an impact model, check it.
  2. Authoring an impact model: the model, and how to change it safely.
  3. Measuring progress: observations, status, and what changed.
  4. Reports and decks: the artifacts for each audience. The problem tree, V2MOM, and DMAIC guides map those projections to the model.
  5. Review round trip: ask reviewers, bring answers back.
  6. Quality and judging: lint, rubrics, and judges.
  7. MCP server and agent skills: working with an AI agent.
  8. Examples: four fictional, complete examples.
  9. CLI reference: every command, flag convention, and exit code.

For the concepts behind the model, see the research brief; for how each concept maps to a Go type, see Concepts to Go types.

docs.title: Authoring an Impact Model
docs.text: An impact model is one document of connected elements. This guide describes the elements, how they refer to each other, and the ways to change them.

docs.title: The elements
docs.text:
Element What it is Outcome A change that should happen, at one of five levels: output, short_term, medium_term, long_term, or impact Link A causal arrow from one outcome to another, with a rationale and a polarity. A feedback link marks a loop Group Preconditions for an outcome: all of them, any of them, or at least k of n. Groups can nest Intervention Something the program does to bring about outcomes Assumption Something that must hold for a link or outcome to work, with a criticality and a status Indicator How an outcome, activity, or assumption is measured, with a baseline, targets, and a frequency. It can also be worked out from other indicators, such as a cost per outcome Actor A person or organization who changes, delivers, or co-owns an outcome Evidence A source that supports or contradicts an element, with a sensitivity Pathway A named route through the impact model, such as one program's or product's contribution, with the North Star it steers by Cause, effect, target group The problem tree: causes below the core problem (context.problemStatement), effects above it, each linked to others through parents, and the groups affected. Outcomes say which causes they address and which effects they relieve. See the problem tree guide Audience, theme Who needs to see what reported, the short list of numbers each is told, and the codebook for coding stories Metric, term A shared metric library, and a glossary of the words the impact model uses Risk, decision, factor, consultation What could go wrong, what is awaiting a decision, external factors, and the review trail

An outcome also records its responsibility: own, shared, partner, or unaddressed, so a report can separate what the organization answers for from what it only monitors. The document names a ceiling of accountability, the level above which outcomes are tracked but not claimed.

Every ID is a lowercase kebab-case slug, unique across the document, and references are by ID.

docs.title: What a program steers by, and what each audience is told
docs.text:
These choices sit on top of the chain from activities to impact. They are different things, and an impact model can make all of them.

  • Projections on a pathway mark what else it is meant for. projections: [dmaic] marks a program measured often enough to improve with DMAIC; lint then checks its indicators' cadence and survey sizes. See the DMAIC guide.
  • A North Star is the one number a program or product steers by. It is set on the pathway, with an optional one metric that matters and the guardrails that watch what chasing it could harm. It should measure an outcome at or below the ceiling of accountability, never an output or an activity.
  • A headline list is what an audience is told: a short, ordered list on the audience, each entry an indicator with an optional label and note worded for that reader. The board, funders, and members can each lead with different numbers drawn from the same indicators, and every audience sees the same figure for an indicator.
  • Purpose is context.mission, context.vision, and context.values: why the organization exists, what it works toward, and the principles that guide how it works, most important first. They are not part of the causal chain. A V2MOM needs the vision and at least one value.
# A pathway's North Star, and what watches it
impact-model pathway set impact-model.yaml pw-learning \
  --north-star ind-practice-maturity --guardrails ind-retention-learning

# What the board is told, in order
impact-model audience set impact-model.yaml aud-board --set 'headline=[
  {"indicatorId":"ind-practice-maturity","label":"Leadership practice across members"},
  {"indicatorId":"ind-reach-network"}]'

# Why the organization exists
impact-model patch impact-model.yaml - <<'EOF'
[{"op":"add","path":"/context/mission","value":"Strengthen local nonprofits."}]
EOF

Some of the numbers people ask for are arithmetic on others, such as the cost per applied change. Give that indicator a composedOf, and its value is worked out from the latest value of each part when it has none of its own:

impact-model indicator set impact-model.yaml ind-cost-per-change \
  --composed-op ratio --composed-of ind-cost,ind-changes-applied

A ratio and a difference take exactly two indicators, in order. A composition is arithmetic and not a causal link. See Measuring progress for how the value is worked out and what is withheld, and Quality and judging for the rules that check all of it.

docs.title: Provenance: stated, inferred, or confirmed
docs.text:
Each element carries a basis that says why it is in the impact model:

Basis Meaning stated A source says it. Cite the evidence inferred Our reading of the sources hypothesis A guess to test; the first thing to challenge in review confirmed The people it concerns agreed rejected Considered and set aside; kept on record, left out of diagrams and analysis

Record who decided a confirmed or rejected basis with --decided-by as a group or role, not a personal name, and when with --decided-at.

docs.title: Change an impact model with commands
docs.text:
Every element kind has add, set, and rm:

impact-model outcome add impact-model.yaml --id oc-skills --title "Staff write strong applications" --level short_term
impact-model link add impact-model.yaml --id ln-skills-adoption --from oc-skills --to oc-adoption --rationale "Skilled staff apply more often"
impact-model outcome set impact-model.yaml oc-skills --basis confirmed --decided-by "Program board" --decided-at 2026-04-01
impact-model outcome rm impact-model.yaml oc-skills --cascade

Run impact-model <element> add --help to see every field as a flag.

Each command is compiled to a JSON Patch and applied through the same validated path, which has these guarantees:

  • Atomic. If any step fails, nothing is written.
  • Never worse. A change is rejected if the result would have more structural errors than before. --allow-errors accepts structural errors but never a schema violation.
  • Canonical. The file is rewritten in canonical form in its own format.
  • Previewable. --dry-run prints the resulting document and writes nothing.
  • Honest removal. Removing an element that others refer to is rejected; rm --cascade removes the references as well and tells you what it removed.

docs.title: Change an impact model with a patch
docs.text:
For many changes at once, or from a script or an agent, apply an RFC 6902 JSON Patch:

echo '[{"op":"replace","path":"/outcomes/@oc-skills/title","value":"Staff write strong applications"}]' \
  | impact-model patch impact-model.yaml -

Pointers can address an array element by ID: /outcomes/@oc-skills/title selects the outcome with ID oc-skills, and /outcomes/- appends. The patch is applied to a copy, and all of the guarantees above apply.

docs.title: Keep a revision log
docs.text:
When an impact model changes after review, record why. impact-model diff compares two versions by element ID, so a retitled outcome is one changed element, and the same impact model in YAML and JSON has no differences:

impact-model diff impact-model-v1.yaml impact-model-v2.yaml
impact-model diff impact-model-v1.yaml impact-model-v2.yaml --revision --version 0.2 --date 2026-03-01 \
  > revision.patch.json
impact-model patch impact-model-v2.yaml revision.patch.json

--revision prints a patch that appends a draft revision listing every changed element ID. Review it, then apply it.

docs.title: Impact models that belong together
docs.text:
• Parent and child. A program's impact model can contribute to an organization's. validate program.yaml --parent organization.yaml checks that the contributesTo references resolve in the parent.
  • Competing futures. Impact models describing different futures of one market share one actor registry. validate a.yaml b.yaml c.yaml --registry actors.yaml --futures checks that they name their futures and perspectives, do not both speak for the same actor in the same future, and refer to each other's elements correctly. See the competing-futures example.

docs.title: Schemas for editors and agents
docs.text:
The JSON Schemas are generated from the Go types and embedded in the binary:

impact-model schema                                   # list them
impact-model schema impact-model > impact-model.schema.json

Seven schemas are available: theory-of-change, observation-set, impact-model-status, status-diff, actor-registry, review-response, and csv-mapping.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Measuring progress · Quality and judging

docs.title: CLI Reference
docs.text: impact-model <command> --help prints the full help for any command. This page is the map.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
• Output files. -o / --out names the file a command writes. Without it, most commands write to standard output.
  • Observation files. -O / --observations names observation sets, and is repeatable.
  • Dates. --as-of YYYY-MM-DD sets the date a status or report describes.
  • Format. --format text|json is global. graph also takes dot, and export review-packet takes md or docx.
  • Quiet. -q / --quiet prints only problems.
  • Dry run. Commands that change a file take --dry-run, which prints the result and writes nothing.
  • Both formats. An impact model can be YAML or JSON, chosen by extension. Edits keep the file's own format.

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text: Code Meaning 0 Success 1 The input is invalid, a change was rejected, or a check did not pass 2 A usage or I/O error 3 An optional external tool (marp, mmdc, pandoc) is missing

docs.title: Start and format
docs.text: Command What it does init Write a starter impact model that already passes validation fmt Rewrite documents in canonical form (--check, --sort) schema List the seven embedded JSON Schemas or print one

docs.title: Edit
docs.text:
Command What it does <element> add, set, rm Add, change, or remove one element through the validated patch engine patch Apply an RFC 6902 JSON Patch atomically, with @id pointers diff Compare two versions by element ID, or print a draft revision patch

The twenty-one element kinds are actor, assumption, audience, cause, consultation, criterion, decision, effect, evidence, factor, group, indicator, intervention, link, metric, outcome, pathway, risk, target-group, term, and theme. See Authoring an impact model.

docs.title: Check
docs.text: Command What it does validate Schema and structure (--model, --parent, --registry, --futures) lint 72 deterministic rules in three profiles (--profile, --disable, --list) graph Summarize or query the causal graph (--upstream, --downstream, --paths, --cycles, --orphans, --dead-ends, --levels) judge show, record, summary Prepare an impact model for a judge and combine the verdicts

docs.title: Measure
docs.text: Command What it does import observations Load a spreadsheet through a column mapping, reporting every row it cannot place status Compute indicator, outcome, pathway, link, and assumption status as of a date (--prev, --rollup, --tolerance)

docs.title: Report and export
docs.text: Command What it does report <kind> Markdown reports: definition kinds (no data needed) and status kinds deck workshop, exec, learning-review, story Marp slide decks (--export renders with marp) export csv <table> indicators, metrics, glossary, metric-selection, collection-plan export docx, export pptx Word and PowerPoint through mmdc and pandoc export okr, export journey, export v2mom, export dmaic JSON for the PRISM tools; the V2MOM and DMAIC guides say how each maps

docs.title: Review
docs.text: Command What it does export review-packet, export review-sheet Send an impact model out for review import review Turn reviewers' answers into a patch, flagged rows, and a consultation record approve Record approval, with approvers, a version, and a date

docs.title: Serve
docs.text: Command What it does mcp Serve the tools to an AI agent over MCP on standard input and output (--root)

docs.title: Shell completion
docs.text: impact-model completion bash|zsh|fish|powershell prints a completion script.

docs.title: DMAIC
docs.text:
If you already run DMAIC (Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, Control) efforts, this page shows where each part of a DMAIC metrics document comes from in an impact model, how to mark the programs that suit DMAIC, and what the impact model checks before it lets you start.

impact-model export dmaic impact-model.yaml -O observations.yaml -o dmaic.json

The output is a DMAIC metrics document in the JSON format of prism-roadmap's goals/dmaic package, which validates it and can render it as slides or as Markdown for PDF.

docs.title: Which programs suit DMAIC
docs.text:
DMAIC improves a process with statistics: control charts need many measurements taken on a steady schedule. A program whose numbers arrive weekly, such as an online course catalog with completion rates and a post-course survey, suits it. A program measured once a year does not: twenty points would take twenty years.

So DMAIC is opt-in, per pathway. Mark a pathway, the impact model's program or product, with projections:

pathways:
  - id: pw-catalog
    title: Course catalog
    projections:
      - dmaic

Only marked pathways are checked by the DMAIC lint rules and exported.

docs.title: What lint checks first
docs.text:
impact-model lint checks every indicator of a marked pathway:

Rule Checks Why IMP-DMA-001 It has a frequency and a data source (dataSource or collection.system) Without them nothing is measured on a schedule IMP-DMA-002 It is measured at least 20 times a year Control limits need 20 to 25 points; fewer a year means waiting years IMP-DMA-003 A survey indicator gets at least 30 responses per measurement Below 30 a score swings with chance; an NPS needs about 100 for a margin near ±10 points

Responses per measurement are collection.respondentsPerYear, times collection.sampleRate when set, divided by measurements per year. A weekly survey of 6,500 learners a year gives about 125 per week. The same survey of 780 learners gives 15, and lint suggests measuring every month, pooling across courses, or asking more people.

The rules are warnings, not errors: an indicator that fails them can still be exported, but its chart will not be ready for a long time.

docs.title: The mapping at a glance
docs.text: DMAIC Comes from In impact model terms Category each pathway marked dmaic A program or product: a group of outcomes and the interventions that bring them about Metric each indicator of the pathway with a numeric baseline and target An indicator measures one outcome or intervention Metric baseline, target baseline.value, and the value of the latest-dated target Metric current the latest observation, or the baseline before any Metric data points the indicator's observations, given with -O Observations are dated values recorded against an indicator Metric control limits computed from the data points, only from 20 or more Metric trend direction direction: increase, decrease, or maintain Metric status the indicator's health on the status date: Green, Yellow, Red Metric phase derived; see Phases Metric root causes the causes the measured outcome addresses The problem tree: causes, each immediate, underlying, or structural Initiatives the pathway's interventions aimed at the measured outcome An intervention is something the organization does to change an outcome

docs.title: One metric, end to end
docs.text:
The course catalog example is a fictional nonprofit's free on-demand certificate courses. Its North Star is the weekly completion rate:

indicators:
  - id: ind-completion-rate
    measures: oc-mt-certified
    name: Course completion rate
    unit: percent
    direction: increase
    baseline: { value: 38, date: "2025-12-29" }
    targets:
      - { value: 45, date: "2026-12-31" }
      - { value: 50, date: "2027-12-31" }
    dataSource: Learning platform
    frequency: P1W

With 24 weeks of observations it becomes this metric, shown trimmed:

{
  "id": "ind-completion-rate",
  "name": "Course completion rate",
  "baseline": 38,
  "current": 40.9,
  "target": 50,
  "unit": "percent",
  "phase": "Improve",
  "trendDirection": "higher_better",
  "controlLimits": { "ucl": 42.855, "lcl": 35.987, "centerLine": 39.421, "sigma": 1.145 },
  "frequency": "Weekly",
  "dataSource": "Learning platform",
  "status": "Green",
  "dataPoints": [
    { "timestamp": "2026-01-05T00:00:00Z", "value": 38 },
    { "timestamp": "2026-01-12T00:00:00Z", "value": 39 }
  ],
  "rootCauses": [
    { "id": "cause-no-time", "description": "Staff cannot set aside an hour at a time for a course.", "category": "Immediate", "validated": true }
  ],
  "initiativeIds": ["int-course-redesign"]
}
  • The baseline is the indicator's baseline and the target its 2027 target, the latest one.
  • The data points are the 24 weekly observations, and the current value is the last of them.
  • With 24 points, the control limits are computed.
  • The outcome it measures, learners completing courses, addresses the cause "Staff cannot set aside an hour at a time". The cause cites evidence, so it is marked validated.
  • The intervention aimed at that outcome, shortening modules, is in progress, so the metric is in the Improve phase and lists it as its initiative.

docs.title: Data points and the current value
docs.text:
Data points are the indicator's observations from the files given with -O, in date order. An observation broken down by a group, with a disaggregation such as member size: small, describes only that group, so it is not a point on the total's chart and is left out.

The current value is the latest data point. Before there are any, it is the baseline.

docs.title: Control limits
docs.text:
Control limits are those of an individuals chart (I-MR), the usual chart for one measurement per period:

  • the center line is the mean of the data points
  • sigma is estimated as the average moving range, the mean difference between consecutive points, divided by 1.128
  • the upper and lower limits are the center line plus and minus three sigma

They are computed only from 20 or more data points. With fewer the metric has no limits, because limits from a handful of points mislead more than they help.

A point outside the limits is a signal that the process has changed. A metric that is improving on purpose will cross a limit; that is the improvement showing, and the limits should be recomputed from the new level.

Process capability (Cp, Cpk, sigma level) is never filled. It compares the process with specification limits, the bounds a result must stay within, and an impact model records targets, not specification limits.

docs.title: Phases
docs.text:
DMAIC tracks which phase each metric is in. The impact model does not record a phase, so the export derives one, as a convention:

Phase When Control The indicator has achieved its target on the status date. Hold the gain Measure There are fewer than 20 data points, too few for control limits Improve An intervention aimed at the measured outcome is in progress Analyze Otherwise: enough data, the target not yet met, and nothing in progress to change it

Define is never assigned: a metric with a baseline and a target has already been defined.

docs.title: Root causes and initiatives
docs.text:
A metric's root causes are the causes its outcome addresses, from the model's problem tree. Each cause's level becomes the category, such as Immediate or Structural, and a cause that cites evidence is marked validated.

The document's initiatives are the interventions of the marked pathways that aim at a metric's outcome, or that the metric measures directly. Each lists the metrics it should move, and its expected impact names the outcomes it targets.

Initiative status From the intervention Planned planned In Progress in_progress Completed completed Cancelled not exported: a cancelled intervention is not an initiative

A paused intervention is exported with no status. External links come from initiativeRefs, such as a VisionStudio or Jira item.

docs.title: What is left out
docs.text: Left out Why An indicator with no numeric baseline or target, such as a qualitative rating A DMAIC metric is a number moving from a baseline to a target. Each is named on standard error Pathways not marked dmaic They are not DMAIC efforts The causal links, assumptions, and evidence report pathway and report assumptions show them Thresholds and process capability The model records targets, not warning thresholds or specification limits

docs.title: When the export is refused
docs.text:
export dmaic writes nothing and exits with status 2 when no pathway is marked dmaic, or when no indicator of a marked pathway has a numeric baseline and target:

impact-model: impact-model.yaml: the impact model cannot be drawn as DMAIC: mark a pathway with projections: [dmaic]

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Four complete examples are in the repository's examples/ directory. Everything in them is fictional: the organizations, people, numbers, and URLs (all under example.org) are invented for illustration.

Each is valid, is in canonical form, and is checked by the test suite, and the two reference impact models lint with no errors, so you can copy one as a starting point.

docs.title: Membership network
docs.text:
examples/intermediary: Riverbend Nonprofit Network, a network of about 150 nonprofits and eight staff, with three program areas modelled as pathways: Learning Exchange, Shared Services, and Civic Voice.

It shows two impact layers (member change and resident change) with the ceiling of accountability between them; 23 outcomes across all five levels with all, any, and at_least precondition logic; a metric library; measurement design with weighted selection criteria and a collection budget; a problem tree, with causes that feed one another and the effects of the core problem, and target groups; audiences and a story codebook; a mission and vision, a North Star with a guardrail for each program area, and headline lists that lead the board, funders, and members with different numbers; and a spreadsheet import with its column mapping. The folder holds the impact model, a quarter of observations with stories and a learning review, and a monthly CSV with its mapping.yaml.

impact-model status examples/intermediary/impact-model.yaml \
  -O examples/intermediary/observations-2026-q3.yaml
impact-model import observations --csv examples/intermediary/csv/monthly-q4.csv \
  --map examples/intermediary/csv/mapping.yaml --model examples/intermediary/impact-model.yaml

docs.title: Market adoption
docs.text: examples/market-adoption: a fictional open standard driven to adoption in a market with two competing approaches, a proprietary single-vendor scheme and an extension of an older authorization framework. It shows an impact model about a market rather than a program: adoption outcomes, the competition modelled as outcomes in the interest sphere, and a shared actor registry. It uses the Adopt-Adapt-Expand-Respond market-systems framing.

docs.title: Competing futures
docs.text:
examples/competing-futures: three impact models that describe different futures of one market and share one registry of actors. Validate them together:

impact-model validate examples/competing-futures/future-*.yaml \
  --registry examples/competing-futures/actors.yaml --futures

docs.title: Course catalog
docs.text:
examples/course-catalog: a fictional small nonprofit's free, on-demand certificate courses for staff of other nonprofits. Its one program is marked projections: [dmaic] and is measured weekly: completion rate, courses started, hours to a first forum answer, and a post-course Net Promoter Score from a survey large enough for weekly scores. Twenty-four weeks of observations give each of those enough points for control limits. A monthly catalog count and a yearly graduate survey are flagged by the DMAIC lint rules on purpose. Its problem tree has two causes, a missing training budget that leaves staff no time, and two effects, untrained leadership and weaker programs.

impact-model lint examples/course-catalog/impact-model.yaml
impact-model export dmaic examples/course-catalog/impact-model.yaml \
  -O examples/course-catalog/observations-2026-h1.yaml

See the DMAIC guide.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: CLI reference

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
go install github.com/ProductBuildersHQ/impact-model/cmd/impact-model@latest
impact-model --version

The tool is a single Go binary. Three optional programs add output formats; the command that needs one tells you if it is missing and exits with code 3 without writing anything:

Program Needed for Marp (marp) Rendering decks to PDF, PPTX, or HTML Mermaid CLI (mmdc) Diagrams as images in decks and Word documents Pandoc (pandoc) Word and PowerPoint export

Markdown reports, CSV tables, Marp Markdown, and everything that checks or measures an impact model need none of them.

docs.title: Create an impact model
docs.text:
impact-model init --id my-program --name "My program" --out impact-model.yaml

This writes a small starter impact model that already passes validation, with TODO placeholders to replace. An impact model is a YAML or JSON file; the format follows the file extension. Open it in any editor, or change it through the commands in Authoring an impact model.

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
impact-model validate impact-model.yaml   # schema and structure
impact-model lint impact-model.yaml       # is the impact model sound?
impact-model fmt impact-model.yaml        # write it in canonical form

validate says the document is well formed: the schema, duplicate IDs, references that do not resolve, invalid values, bad dates. lint says whether the impact model is sound. A new impact model is GO under --profile draft; the default standard profile also reports warnings.

fmt rewrites a file in canonical form: a stable field order, two-space indentation, and a trailing newline, so diffs stay readable. Formatting is idempotent. YAML comments are not kept, because tool-written files are canonical; put notes in description and narrative fields.

docs.title: Ask questions of the causal graph
docs.text:
impact-model graph impact-model.yaml                      # a summary
impact-model graph impact-model.yaml --orphans            # outcomes nothing leads to
impact-model graph impact-model.yaml --dead-ends          # outcomes that lead nowhere
impact-model graph impact-model.yaml --upstream --from oc-adoption
impact-model graph impact-model.yaml --format dot | dot -Tsvg > graph.svg

docs.title: Get a first report
docs.text:
impact-model report definitions impact-model.yaml --out definitions.md

This renders the pathways, logic models, metric definitions, and glossary as one Markdown document. It needs no observations, so a workshop can review it before any data exists.

To start from the problem rather than the solution, draw the problem tree: the core problem, its causes below, and its effects above. See the problem tree guide.

impact-model report problem-tree impact-model.yaml --out problem-tree.md

docs.title: Measure progress
docs.text:
Once you have numbers, put them in an observation set (see Measuring progress) and ask how far the impact model has come:

impact-model status impact-model.yaml -O observations.yaml
impact-model report exec impact-model.yaml -O observations.yaml -o exec.md

docs.title: Working in a Git repository
docs.text:
Specifications are meant to be diffed and reviewed. Two habits help:

  • Run impact-model fmt --check *.yaml in CI. It exits with code 1 if any file is not in canonical form.
  • Add a .gitattributes line so Windows checkouts keep LF line endings. The canonical form is byte-exact LF, and a checkout that converts to CRLF will look non-canonical.
* text=auto eol=lf
*.csv -text

CSV files exported by the tool follow RFC 4180 and keep their CRLF, so they are left alone.

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text: Code Meaning 0 Success 1 The input is invalid, or a change was rejected, or a check did not pass 2 A usage or I/O error 3 An optional external tool (marp, mmdc, pandoc) is missing

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Read Authoring an impact model, or open a complete impact model in Examples.

docs.title: MCP Server and Agent Skills
docs.text: The same validated operations the command line offers are available to an AI agent over the Model Context Protocol, and five agent skills describe the common workflows.

docs.title: The MCP server
docs.text:
impact-model mcp --root ./impact-models

The server speaks MCP over standard input and output. Configure an MCP client to run that command; for example, in a client that takes a JSON configuration:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "impact-model": {
      "command": "impact-model",
      "args": ["mcp", "--root", "./impact-models"]
    }
  }
}

It makes no network calls and no model calls.

docs.title: Tools
docs.text:
Tool What it does impact_schema List the embedded JSON Schemas or return one impact_validate Validate an impact model impact_lint Lint an impact model with a profile impact_graph Query the causal graph impact_status Compute a status snapshot from observations impact_report Render a definition or status report impact_deck Generate a deck as Marp Markdown impact_diff Compare two versions of an impact model impact_judge_bundle Build the judge bundle impact_patch Apply a JSON Patch, atomically

A tool takes an impact model inline (the document argument) or by path. impact_patch rejects any patch that adds validation errors, exactly as the patch command does, so an agent cannot leave an impact model worse than it found it.

docs.title: Where an agent can read and write
docs.text: A path must lie inside --root, which defaults to the current directory. These are refused with the same answer on every platform: a path with a .. element, a rooted or drive path outside the root, and a symbolic link that leads outside the root. An inline document is limited in size.

docs.title: Agent skills
docs.text:
A skill is a Markdown file that tells an agent how to carry out one task with the commands above. They live in the repository's skills/ directory.

Skill Use it to impact-draft-from-sources Draft an impact model for an organization from its public pages and reports. Every source is recorded as evidence, and every element is labelled stated, inferred, or hypothesis impact-author Add, change, or remove outcomes, links, assumptions, indicators, actors, and other elements with validated edits impact-status-refresh Load a new period's numbers from a spreadsheet, then report where the impact model stands and what changed impact-learning-review Prepare and record a learning review for a period impact-audience-story Draft a short update for one audience from the impact model's numbers and consented stories

Each skill is tested: the commands and flags it names must exist, and its sequence of steps is run against the examples to check it works and repeats.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Examples · CLI reference

docs.title: Measuring Progress
docs.text: An impact model says what you expect. Measuring says how far you have come. The measurement is a pure function of three inputs: the impact model, the observations, and a date. The same inputs always give the same answer.

docs.title: Indicators
docs.text:
An indicator says how an outcome (or an assumption) is measured. It carries a baseline, targets with dates, a collection frequency, and the direction that counts as progress (increase or decrease). A quantitative indicator has numbers; a qualitative one has ordered levels, such as Emerging to Embedded.

Indicators can use a shared metric from the library, so the same measure is defined once. A metric says how values combine across pathways: sum, mean, weighted_mean, median, mode, min, max, latest, or none for a count that cannot be added up, such as distinct people. An indicator can also roll up from other indicators; a direct observation always beats a roll-up.

An indicator's claim says what the organization can say about it: attribution (we caused this) or contribution (we contributed to it). The default is contribution.

docs.title: Where an indicator sits in the chain
docs.text:
What an indicator measures decides its tier, which is never stored:

Tier The indicator measures For example activity an intervention hours delivered, dollars spent output an output-level outcome people reached outcome a short-term, medium-term, or long-term outcome skills gained, practice applied. These are the driver metrics impact an impact outcome residents served, reported as a contribution

Resources are measured as activity-tier indicators with a unit such as hours or dollars. impact-model report metric-tree lays a pathway's indicators out in this order.

docs.title: North Star, guardrails, and headline lists
docs.text:
Three choices sit on top of the tiers, and they are different things:

  • A North Star is the one number a program or product steers by. Set it in the pathway's focus, with an optional oneMetricId and the guardrailIds that watch what pursuing it could harm. It should measure an outcome at or below the ceiling of accountability, never an output or an activity.
  • A headline list is what an audience is told: a short, ordered list on the audience, each entry an indicator with an optional label and note worded for that reader. Every audience sees the same figure for an indicator; only the label and note differ. A North Star may lead one list and not appear in another.
  • Purpose is context.mission and context.vision, plain statements. They are not part of the causal chain.

impact-model report headline shows what each audience is told, and the story report and deck use the same lists. impact-model lint checks all of it: the TOC-NSM-*, TOC-HLN-*, IMP-AUD-002, and IMP-CTX-001 rules.

docs.title: Working a metric out from others
docs.text:
Some of the numbers people ask for are arithmetic on others, such as the cost per applied change. Give that indicator a composedOf:

composedOf:
  op: ratio              # ratio, difference, product, or sum
  indicatorIds: [ind-cost, ind-changes-applied]   # cost divided by changes

A ratio and a difference take exactly two indicators, in order. When the indicator has no observation of its own, its value is worked out from the latest value of each part, and it is marked as an estimate if any part is. If a part is missing, or a divisor is zero, there is no value and nothing is guessed. A composition is arithmetic, not a causal link, and an indicator is either composed or rolled up, not both.

docs.title: Observations
docs.text:
Measurements go in an observation set, a separate file that refers to the Impact model by ID:

kind: ObservationSet
specVersion: "0.1"
modelId: riverbend-network
period: 2026-Q3
observations:
  - indicatorId: ind-hours-learning
    date: "2026-09-30"
    value: 3650
    source: Attendance sheets
    quality: verified

An observation has a date and either a value (quantitative) or a level (qualitative), plus a source, a quality (verified, reported, or estimated), and an optional note. The same file also holds:

  • Assumption assessments: whether an assumption is still holding.
  • Stories: a person's account, with the consent that was given and a sensitivity. See consent.
  • Learning reviews: what changed in a period, the surprises, and decisions.
  • Notes: context that belongs with the numbers.

Check a set against the impact model it measures:

impact-model validate observations-2026-q3.yaml --model impact-model.yaml

docs.title: Load a spreadsheet
docs.text:
Most programs already keep their numbers in a spreadsheet. Describe its columns once in a mapping file, then import:

modelId: riverbend-network
period: 2026-Q4
dateFormat: 02/01/2006
columns:
  indicator: Measure
  date: Month end
  value: Value
  pathway: Program
  quality: Quality
  source: Source
indicatorAliases:
  Leadership practice maturity: ind-practice-maturity
metricAliases:
  Attendee hours: met-attendee-hours

impact-model import observations --csv q4.csv --map mapping.yaml --model impact-model.yaml \
  --out obs-q4.yaml --unmatched q4-unmatched.csv

A row can name an indicator directly, through an alias, or through a metric plus a pathway. Every row either becomes an observation or is reported as unmatched with its row number and the reason; nothing is dropped silently. Unmatched rows are written to --unmatched as a sheet you can fix and import again. The exit code is 1 when some rows were unmatched (the rest are still written).

docs.title: Status
docs.text:
impact-model status impact-model.yaml -O obs-q3.yaml -O obs-q4.yaml --as-of 2026-12-31 --out status-q4.json

status prints a summary. --format json prints the full snapshot, and --out writes it to a file. The date defaults to the latest observation.

docs.title: Indicator status
docs.text:
For each indicator the snapshot gives its progress against what the targets call for by the date:

Status Meaning achieved The latest value has reached the target on_track At or within tolerance of the expected progress at_risk Behind expected progress by more than the tolerance off_track Far behind, or moving the wrong way stale The newest observation is older than twice the collection frequency no_data Nothing observed, and the first target date has passed not_started Nothing yet, before the first target date baseline_only No targets to measure against

--tolerance (default 0.10) sets how far behind still counts as on track.

docs.title: Outcome and pathway status
docs.text: An outcome's status combines its indicators (--rollup worst, the default, or mean) with the state of what leads to it. Pathway status follows the precondition logic: an all group takes its worst member, any its best, and at_least k the k-th best. A negative link, an inhibitor, caps its target at at_risk while its source is on track.

docs.title: Assumptions and confidence
docs.text: An assumption assessed as at risk caps every link and outcome that depends on it at at_risk; a critical assumption that is invalidated caps them at off_track. Each link gets a rule-based confidence score from its evidence, its assumptions, and whether it has a rationale. Confidence for a route to impact is derived from its links, so a weak link shows up where it matters.

docs.title: What changed
docs.text:
Keep each snapshot and compare:

impact-model status impact-model.yaml -O obs-q4.yaml --prev status-q3.json
impact-model report exec impact-model.yaml -O obs-q4.yaml --prev status-q3.json

The comparison lists the indicators, outcomes, links, and assumptions whose status or confidence changed, and the elements that were added or removed.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Reports and decks

docs.title: Problem Tree
docs.text:
A problem tree puts the problem a program exists to solve in the middle, its causes below as roots, and its effects above as branches. It comes before the theory of change: the roots say what the program could work on, and the branches say what harm it should reduce. Drawn from an impact model, it is one more projection of the same model, and it checks the solution against the problem: every cause and every effect should be addressed by an outcome or set aside with a reason.

impact-model report problem-tree impact-model.yaml        # Markdown, with a Mermaid diagram
impact-model report problem-tree-d2 impact-model.yaml     # the same, with a D2 diagram
impact-model report problem-tree-json impact-model.yaml   # the diagram document itself, as JSON

docs.title: The parts and where they live
docs.text:
Diagram In the model Notes Core problem, in the middle context.problemStatement The problem the program responds to Causes (roots), below causes Each with a level: immediate, underlying, or structural A cause leading to another a cause's parents The causes it contributes to; none means it leads straight to the core problem Effects (branches), above effects What the core problem leads to An effect leading to another an effect's parents The effects it follows from; none means it follows straight from the core problem What addresses a cause an outcome's addressesCauses Usually earlier outcomes: what the program works on What relieves an effect an outcome's addressesEffects Usually long-term and impact outcomes: the harm the program reduces Set aside outOfScope.reason on a cause or effect Real, but not something this program takes on

The impact model is JSON first: a model file is JSON or YAML, read against one JSON Schema generated from the Go types.

context:
  problemStatement: Poor eating health
causes:
  - id: cause-busy
    statement: Too busy to cook
    level: immediate
  - id: cause-fast-food
    statement: Fast food is everywhere
    level: underlying
    parents: [cause-busy]
  - id: cause-poverty
    statement: Poverty
    level: structural
    outOfScope:
      reason: Beyond what this program can change.
effects:
  - id: eff-diabetes
    statement: Diabetes and heart disease
  - id: eff-costs
    statement: Higher health costs
    parents: [eff-diabetes]
outcomes:
  - id: oc-time-to-cook
    title: People have time to cook
    level: short_term
    addressesCauses: [cause-busy]
  - id: oc-eat-well
