docs.title: Release Notes v0.1.0
docs.text:
Released: 2026-10-30

The first release. A Go-first model of a Theory of Change, with generated JSON Schemas, a command line, an MCP server, measurement, reports and decks, and a review round trip, all working on one validated document.

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• A model you can trust. Outcomes, causal links, precondition groups, interventions, assumptions, indicators, actors, evidence, and pathways, with a provenance for every element: stated, inferred, hypothesis, confirmed, or rejected.
  • Safe editing. One validated, atomic patch engine behind the CLI, the SDK, and the MCP tools. A change that would leave a theory worse is rejected.
  • Quality checks. Seven embedded JSON Schemas, structural validation, 48 deterministic lint rules in three profiles, and a rubric for LLM-as-a-Judge review.
  • Measurement. Indicator, outcome, pathway, link, and assumption status as of a date, with assumption propagation and rule-based confidence.
  • Artifacts for every audience. Logic models, outcome maps, results frameworks, executive and audience reports, four slide decks, and Word, PowerPoint, and CSV export.
  • Review that comes back. Send a packet or sheet out, bring the answers back as proposed changes, and record approval.
  • Agent ready. An MCP server with ten tools and five agent skills.

docs.title: Model and schema
docs.text:
• Five outcome levels, precondition groups (all, any, at_least, nested), causal links with polarity and feedback loops, and a ceiling of accountability.
  • Responsibility for each outcome (own, shared, partner, unaddressed), a problem tree, target groups, audiences, and a story codebook.
  • A shared metric library with aggregation rules, a glossary, a collection plan, and a measurement budget.
  • Seven JSON Schemas generated from the Go types and embedded for editors and agents: theory-of-change, observation-set, theory-of-change-status, status-diff, actor-registry, review-response, and csv-mapping.
  • Parent and child theories, and competing futures that share one actor registry.
  • Canonical YAML and JSON, so the same theory is byte-identical however it is written, and a content hash that is the same in every export.

docs.title: Editing
docs.text:
• add, set, and rm for twenty element kinds, and patch for RFC 6902 JSON Patches with @id pointers. Changes are atomic and previewable with --dry-run; rm --cascade removes what cannot survive the removal.
  • diff compares two versions by element ID and can draft a revision record.
  • fmt writes canonical form; init writes a starter theory.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• validate for schema and structure, observation sets, children against a parent, and competing futures.
  • lint with 48 rules, profiles draft, standard, and full, and a structured-evaluation report as JSON.
  • graph for upstream and downstream queries, paths, cycles, orphans, dead ends, and levels, with Graphviz output.
  • judge show, record, and summary for a core rubric of 12 categories and a development addendum, with four aggregation modes. The commands make no model calls.

docs.title: Measurement
docs.text:
• import observations loads a spreadsheet through a column mapping and reports every row it cannot place.
  • status gives each indicator a status (achieved, on_track, at_risk, off_track, stale, no_data, not_started, baseline_only), rolls indicators up to outcomes and pathways by the precondition logic, caps results by assumption status, and scores confidence. Comparing to an earlier snapshot lists what changed.

docs.title: Reports, decks, and exports
docs.text:
• 11 definition reports that need no data, and 12 status reports, including a story report per audience and a learning review. Stories and quotes are shown only with consent, and restricted evidence is never rendered.
  • Four Marp decks (workshop, executive, learning review, audience story) with speaker notes.
  • CSV tables, Word and PowerPoint through mmdc and pandoc, and OKR and outcome-journey JSON for the PRISM tools.

docs.title: Review round trip
docs.text:
• export review-packet and export review-sheet send a theory out.
  • import review turns answers into a patch, a list of rows for a person, and a consultation record, and never changes the theory itself.
  • approve records approval with approvers, a version, and a date, and refuses while hypotheses remain open.

docs.title: MCP server and skills
docs.text:
• theoryofchange mcp serves ten tools over standard input and output. File paths are confined to a root directory, including symbolic links.
  • Five agent skills: draft a theory from sources, author and edit, refresh status from a spreadsheet, run a learning review, and write an audience story.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Three fictional, complete examples: a membership network, a market-adoption theory, and three competing futures. The test suite checks that each is valid, in canonical form, and free of real URLs.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
• The documentation site has user guides for getting started, authoring, measuring, reports and decks, the review round trip, quality and judging, and the MCP server, plus a CLI reference.
  • The research brief, concepts-to-types map, and the product and technical specifications are published alongside.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
go install github.com/ProductBuildersHQ/impact-model/cmd/impact-model@v0.1.0

Go 1.26.5 or later. Three optional programs add output formats: marp for decks, mmdc for diagrams, and pandoc for Word and PowerPoint. A command that needs one that is missing writes nothing and exits with code 3.

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text:
This is the first release, so there is nothing to migrate. Document and observation files carry specVersion: "0.1". Exit codes are 0 for success, 1 for invalid input or a rejected change, 2 for a usage or I/O error, and 3 for a missing external tool.

On Windows, keep LF line endings for theory files (* text=auto eol=lf in .gitattributes): the canonical form is byte-exact LF.

docs.title: Known Limitations
docs.text:
• Sharing a review through Google Docs and Sheets is not built into this tool. It makes no network calls; the gogoogle command line covers the Google side, and an agent skill that runs the whole workflow is planned.
  • The integration contract for USM and UFM is a draft awaiting review by their owners.
  • Rendering diagrams to PNG, and decks to PPTX, needs mmdc and marp. The test suite skips those paths when the tools are absent.
  • Judging needs a judge. The tool prepares the bundle and combines verdicts but does not call a model.

docs.title: Release Notes v0.2.0
docs.text:
Released: 2026-11-01

Ties the chain from activities to impact to the numbers people steer by and are told. A program or product can name a North Star and the guardrails that watch it, each audience can lead with its own short list of numbers, and 18 new lint rules check that the chain is filled in. The logic model can now be drawn as columns with a real arrow wherever one thing leads to another.

This release has one breaking change: the intermediate outcome level is now medium_term. See Upgrading.

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• Headline metrics. A North Star, an optional one metric that matters, and guardrails for each program or product. A short, ordered, worded headline list for each audience, drawn from the same indicators, so the board, funders, and members can lead with different numbers and still see the same figure.
  • A checked chain. 66 lint rules, 18 of them new, that look for an activity that leads nowhere, a link and intervention that disagree, an audience told about outcomes but given no numbers, and a North Star that is an output or sits above the ceiling of accountability.
  • A layered logic model diagram. Columns from inputs to impact, a box for each item, and arrows that follow the theory. Written as D2 and as Mermaid.
  • Composed indicators. A number such as cost per applied change is worked out from the latest value of its parts, and an estimate is shown as an estimate.
  • One series of levels. Short, medium, and long term, with medium_term replacing intermediate.

docs.title: Headline metrics
docs.text:
• North Star. A pathway's focus names the indicator it steers by (northStarId), an optional oneMetricId, the guardrailIds that watch what chasing it could harm, and a rationale. A pathway can now be a program or a product.
  • Headline lists. An audience's headline is an ordered list of indicators, each with an optional label and note worded for that reader.
  • Mission and vision. context.mission and context.vision state purpose without making it part of the causal chain.
  • Tiers. What an indicator measures decides its tier (activity, output, outcome, or impact). Document.IndicatorTier, IndicatorServes, and IndicatorPathways answer it once for every rule and report.
  • Commands. pathway set takes --north-star, --one-metric, and --guardrails, and an audience's headline list is set with --set headline=.... Removing an indicator with rm --cascade also removes it from every headline list and focus that names it.

docs.title: Lint
docs.text:
18 new rules, 66 in all:

  • The chain (TOC-INT-003 to TOC-INT-007): every intervention says what it produces, leads to an impact, agrees with the links that name it, is measured, and states its resources.
  • Headline lists (TOC-AUD-002, TOC-HLN-001 to TOC-HLN-004): an audience told about outcomes is also given numbers, and a headline list is short, is reported to its audience, can be produced, and is chosen when there are many indicators.
  • North Stars (TOC-NSM-001 to TOC-NSM-007): a North Star measures an outcome at or below the ceiling of accountability, has a baseline, a target, and a guardrail, belongs to its own pathway, and is not also a guardrail.
  • Framing (TOC-CTX-001): the theory states its mission or vision.

Every new rule is a warning or advice, so a theory that was GO stays GO.

docs.title: Reports and decks
docs.text:
• headline shows what each audience is told, with the latest figure, status, claim, notes, and caveats, and a matrix of who is told what. --audience narrows it.
  • metric-tree shows, for each pathway, its North Star and guardrails and then its indicators from activity to impact, as a table and a diagram. --pathway narrows it.
  • logic-model-layered and logic-model-d2 draw the logic model as columns. See below.
  • Estimates. An estimated value reads "estimate, on 2026-09-30" in every report, with its observation note.
  • Story report and deck. They tell an audience its whole headline list, in its order and wording. They no longer take the first five indicators in file order.
  • Workshop deck. Each logic model table is followed by a slide that draws the same logic model as columns with arrows.

docs.title: The layered logic model diagram
docs.text:
An input leads to the activities that use it, an activity to the outputs it lists and then to the outcomes it targets, and an outcome to the outcomes its causal links point to, so one box can lead to several and several can lead to one. Within a column, boxes are ordered to keep arrows from crossing. A link that runs back to an earlier stage is feedback. It is listed under the diagram and not drawn across the boxes in between.

logic-model-layered writes Mermaid. logic-model-d2 writes D2, and its grid keeps every stage in its own column:

theoryofchange report logic-model-d2 theory.yaml --pathway pw-learning > lm.d2
d2 lm.d2 lm.svg

The existing logic-model table and --diagram are unchanged. The diagram is written through d2vision's diagram spec.

docs.title: Composed indicators
docs.text: An indicator can be worked out from others with composedOf: a ratio, difference, product, or sum, such as a cost divided by the changes it paid for. When the indicator has no observation of its own, its value comes from the latest value of each part, and it is marked as an estimate if any part is. A missing part or a zero divisor gives no value, so a partial figure is never passed off as complete. Validation checks the operation, the number of parts, that the parts exist, and that the arithmetic is not circular. It is arithmetic and not a causal link. indicator set takes --composed-op and --composed-of.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: The membership network example now has a mission and vision, a North Star and guardrail for three of its program areas, and headline lists for the board, funders, and members.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
• The guides cover tiers, North Stars, headline lists, and composed indicators, how a composed value is worked out, the new reports and the layered diagram, and the new lint rules.
  • Diagrams in the README and the docs index show how the chain, its metrics, and each audience's headline numbers fit together.
  • A credits page lists the methods and projects the specification builds on, and THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md carries the license notices of the dependencies compiled into the command line.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
go install github.com/ProductBuildersHQ/impact-model/cmd/impact-model@v0.2.0

Go 1.26.5 or later. The optional programs are the same as in v0.1.0: marp for decks, mmdc for diagrams, and pandoc for Word and PowerPoint. To draw the D2 diagram you also need the d2 tool, and the command that writes D2 does not.

docs.title: intermediate is now medium_term
docs.text:
The level is renamed so that short, medium, and long term read as one series. There is no alias. A theory that still says level: intermediate fails validation, once for each such outcome:

error VAL-SCH-001 /outcomes/6/level: value must be one of 'impact', 'long_term', 'medium_term', 'short_term', 'output'

Replace level: intermediate with level: medium_term in YAML, or "level": "intermediate" with "level": "medium_term" in JSON. Other places that change with it:

  • Reports and diagrams say "Medium-term outcomes" where they said "Intermediate outcomes", and a Mermaid subgraph is lv_medium_term.
  • In Go, toc.LevelIntermediate is toc.LevelMediumTerm.
  • The embedded theory-of-change JSON Schema lists medium_term.

docs.title: More lint findings
docs.text: A theory that was clean can now show new warnings and advice, such as TOC-INT-003 for an intervention that does not say what it produces, and TOC-NSM-007 for a program with no North Star. None is an error, so the result is still GO. Use lint --disable to skip a rule you do not want yet.

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text: Files still carry specVersion: "0.1". This version reads any 0.x, so a document written for v0.1.0 is read, and only its intermediate levels need to change. Every new field is optional. Exit codes are unchanged.

docs.title: Known Limitations
docs.text:
• Inputs are text. The diagram's inputs come from an intervention's free-text resources, so one funding source cannot yet feed several activities by ID.
  • Wide diagrams. With seven stages and long labels the layered diagram is wide, and text on a slide is small. Labels are not wrapped.
  • Feedback is listed, not drawn. A link that runs back to an earlier stage appears in a list under the diagram.
  • Mermaid places its own columns. Only the D2 form keeps each stage in a column.
  • Panels. A slide with panels for background, goal, issues, assumptions, and critical success factors around the diagram is not built.
  • The limitations of v0.1.0 for Google sharing, the USM and UFM contract, rendering tools, and judging still apply.

docs.title: Release Notes v0.3.0
docs.text:
Released: 2026-11-01

The project is now impact-model, an AI-native format from ProductBuildersHQ. One impact model holds the outcomes and causal links of a program, the assumptions and evidence behind them, the interventions that bring them about, how progress is measured, and who is told which numbers. The theory of change, the logic model, the outcome map, the logframe, and OKRs are projections of that one model, each made for a different reader, and none of them is a part of another.

This is the first release under the new module path and command. It renames names only: the format, the lint checks, the reports, and their output are the same as in v0.2.0. A document written for v0.2.0 needs a new kind and a few renamed fields. See Upgrading.

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• One model, many projections. The README and the docs index lead with the impact model as the format, list its projections and the command that draws each, and explain why a logic model is a projection beside the theory of change and not a part of it. A V2MOM projection is planned.
  • A new module path and command. github.com/ProductBuildersHQ/impact-model, and the impact-model command.
  • The decision is recorded. ADR 0001 says what changed, what did not, and which other names were considered.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
go install github.com/ProductBuildersHQ/impact-model/cmd/impact-model@v0.3.0

Go 1.26.5 or later. The optional programs are the same as in v0.2.0: marp for decks, mmdc and d2 for diagrams, and pandoc for Word and PowerPoint.

docs.title: Every renamed name
docs.text:
Was Is module github.com/ProductBuildersHQ/theoryofchange-spec github.com/ProductBuildersHQ/impact-model command theoryofchange impact-model packages pkg/toc, pkg/tocio pkg/impact, pkg/impactio type toc.Document, toc.NewDocument impact.Model, impact.NewModel kind: TheoryOfChange kind: ImpactModel kind: TheoryOfChangeStatus kind: ImpactModelStatus schemas theory-of-change, theory-of-change-status impact-model, impact-model-status file name theory.yaml impact-model.yaml fields tocId, childToc modelId, childModel cross-document reference toc:<id>#<element> model:<id>#<element> lint rule IDs such as TOC-STR-001 IMP-STR-001 flag --toc --model MCP tools toc_* impact_* agent skills toc-* impact-* documentation site productbuildershq.com/theoryofchange-spec productbuildershq.com/impact-model

There are no aliases. The old command, kinds, and field names are not accepted.

docs.title: Documents
docs.text:
A document that still says kind: TheoryOfChange is refused:

error VAL-SCH-003 /kind: invalid document: unknown kind "TheoryOfChange"

To upgrade a document written for v0.2.0:

  1. Change kind: TheoryOfChange to kind: ImpactModel, and kind: TheoryOfChangeStatus to kind: ImpactModelStatus.
  2. Rename the fields tocId to modelId and childToc to childModel.
  3. Change cross-document references from toc: to model:.
  4. If the document was written for v0.1.0, also change level: intermediate to level: medium_term, as described in the v0.2.0 notes.

specVersion stays "0.1", so nothing else in a document changes. Renaming theory.yaml to impact-model.yaml is optional; commands take any file name.

docs.title: Go code
docs.text:
Replace the import paths, then the package and type names:

import (
    "github.com/ProductBuildersHQ/impact-model/pkg/impact"
    "github.com/ProductBuildersHQ/impact-model/pkg/impactio"
)

m := impact.NewModel("my-program", "Too few residents find stable work") // was toc.NewDocument

docs.title: Scripts, configuration, and agents
docs.text:
• Call impact-model where scripts called theoryofchange, and pass --model where they passed --toc.
  • lint --disable names rules as IMP-....
  • An MCP client configuration starts impact-model mcp, and an agent calls the impact_* tools.
  • Copy the skills again from skills/: they are now impact-author, impact-audience-story, impact-draft-from-sources, impact-learning-review, and impact-status-refresh.

docs.title: What did not change
docs.text:
• The projections keep their method names. report pathway, logic-model, outcome-map, and logframe are still the names of those reports.
  • Behavior. Validation, the lint rules, measurement, reports, and decks work as in v0.2.0. Only the names in their output change: a report or message says impact model where it said theory or Theory of Change. The workshop deck keeps Theory of Change in its title.
  • The quality rubric and the specification template in spec/ are still the theory of change checklist and outline.
  • Earlier releases. v0.1.0 and v0.2.0 stay published under the old module path. GitHub redirects the old repository address.

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text: Breaking, for names only. Files still carry specVersion: "0.1", and this version reads any 0.x once the kind and fields are renamed. Exit codes are unchanged. The command still has the same dependencies.

docs.title: Known Limitations
docs.text: The limitations of v0.2.0 still apply.

docs.title: Release Notes v0.4.0
docs.text:
Released: 2026-11-01

Two strategy and improvement formats join the projections of an impact model. A V2MOM is drawn from the model's vision, values, and pathways, and a DMAIC metrics document from the programs measured often enough to improve with statistics. The README now says what the format is: a causal model that states which interventions should change which outcomes, and why.

This release is additive for documents and the command line. One Go function, prismx.ToOKR, returns a type from a different module; see Upgrading.

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• V2MOM. export v2mom writes the vision and values from the context, one method per pathway with its interventions as projects, measures from each pathway's North Star and guardrails, and obstacles from risks and the assumptions not yet shown to hold.
  • DMAIC. Mark a pathway projections: [dmaic], and lint checks that its indicators are measured often enough and from enough people. export dmaic writes each indicator as a metric with its observations, control limits once there are enough points, root causes, improvement initiatives, and a phase.
  • A course catalog example. A fictional nonprofit's free on-demand courses, run with DMAIC on weekly completion with a post-course survey as guardrail.

docs.title: V2MOM projection
docs.text:
impact-model export v2mom impact-model.yaml -O observations.yaml -o v2mom.json
V2MOM From the impact model Vision context.vision Values context.values, new in this release, in order Methods one per pathway; its interventions are the method's projects Measures each pathway's North Star, one metric that matters, and guardrails Obstacles risks, and high or critical assumptions not yet shown to hold, by their assessed status with -O

A model without a vision, values, or a pathway is refused with a message naming what to add. The V2MOM guide maps each part and follows one pathway from the model to the V2MOM.

docs.title: DMAIC projection
docs.text:
pathways:
  - id: pw-catalog
    projections:
      - dmaic

impact-model lint impact-model.yaml
impact-model export dmaic impact-model.yaml -O observations.yaml -o dmaic.json

Three new lint rules check the indicators of a pathway marked for DMAIC, and only those:

  • IMP-DMA-001: it states a frequency and a data source
  • IMP-DMA-002: it is measured at least 20 times a year
  • IMP-DMA-003: a survey indicator gets at least 30 responses per measurement

The export makes each marked pathway a category and each indicator with a numeric baseline and target a metric. Observations become data points, without disaggregated slices, and control limits are those of an individuals chart, computed only from 20 or more points. Root causes come from the problem tree, initiatives from the pathway's interventions, and the phase is derived by a documented convention. Process capability is not filled, because an impact model records targets and not specification limits. The DMAIC guide explains each part.

docs.title: Model additions
docs.text:
• context.values: the principles that guide how the organization works, most important first. A value needs a name (VAL-DOC-006), and names are unique (VAL-DOC-007).
  • pathway.projections: what else a pathway is meant for. Its one value is dmaic. An unknown or repeated projection is reported (VAL-PTH-007).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: examples/course-catalog is new: a pathway marked for DMAIC, weekly platform, survey, and forum indicators, and 24 weeks of observations. Some indicators are flagged by the DMAIC lint rules on purpose. The intermediary example gains values, so it exports as a V2MOM.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
• The README and the docs index describe the impact model as a causal model, and show V2MOM and DMAIC as available projections.
  • New V2MOM and DMAIC guides, written for readers who already know those formats.
  • The glossary says how each projection names an intervention: an activity in the logic model and a project in V2MOM, delivered by initiatives linked through initiativeRefs.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
go install github.com/ProductBuildersHQ/impact-model/cmd/impact-model@v0.4.0

Go 1.26.5 or later. The optional programs are the same as in v0.3.0.

docs.title: Documents and the command line
docs.text: Nothing to change. Every new field is optional, specVersion stays "0.1", and the OKR export writes the same JSON as before. A model that was GO stays GO: the new lint rules only check pathways marked for DMAIC.

docs.title: Go code that calls prismx.ToOKR
docs.text:
The OKR types moved from structured-goals into prism-roadmap, where the other PRISM tools use them, and structured-goals is deprecated. ToOKR now returns *okr.OKRDocument from the new package. Change the import:

// was: import "github.com/grokify/structured-goals/okr"
import "github.com/grokify/prism-roadmap/goals/okr"

The fields and the JSON they write are the same.

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text: An API comparison against v0.3.0 reports the new types and functions above as compatible changes, and one incompatible change: the result type of prismx.ToOKR. Dependencies: prism-roadmap v0.22.0 and prism-core v0.6.0, and structured-goals is no longer used.

docs.title: Known Limitations
docs.text:
• Disaggregated observations. The status of an indicator can take a disaggregated observation, one for a single group, as its latest overall value. This affects reports and the OKR and V2MOM exports; the DMAIC export leaves such observations out. What a disaggregated observation means for the overall status is not yet specified.
  • V2MOM dates. A model with no created or updated date exports them as the zero time, because the V2MOM format does not omit an empty date.
  • DMAIC phases are derived by convention; the model does not record them.
  • The limitations of v0.3.0 still apply.

docs.title: Release Notes v0.5.0
docs.text:
Released: 2026-11-01

The problem tree joins the projections of an impact model. It puts the problem a program exists to solve in the middle, its causes below as roots, and its effects above as branches, and checks that every cause and effect is addressed by an outcome or set aside with a reason. Causes, and the new effects, form a network: each can lead to several others.

This release has one breaking change: a cause's parent is now parents, a list. See Upgrading.

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• Problem trees. report problem-tree draws the core problem with causes below and effects above, arrows flowing upward from the deepest causes to the furthest effects, and lists what addresses each.
  • Effects. The problem tree's branches: what the core problem leads to. Outcomes name the effects they relieve with addressesEffects.
  • A network, not only a tree. A cause can contribute to several others and an effect can follow from several, so parents is a list.
  • JSON first. The diagram is built as a JSON diagram document, from which D2 and Mermaid are rendered, and report problem-tree-json prints it.

docs.title: Problem tree reports
docs.text:
impact-model report problem-tree impact-model.yaml        # Markdown, with a Mermaid diagram
impact-model report problem-tree-d2 impact-model.yaml     # the same, with a D2 diagram
impact-model report problem-tree-json impact-model.yaml   # the diagram document itself
Diagram In the model Core problem, in the middle context.problemStatement Causes (roots), below causes, each leading to its parents or to the core problem Effects (branches), above effects, each following from its parents or from the core problem What addresses a cause an outcome's addressesCauses What relieves an effect an outcome's addressesEffects

The core problem is in the middle row. A cause is one row below its lowest parent and an effect one row above its highest, so every arrow points up. A cause or effect set aside is drawn faded, and a rejected one is left out. The JSON report is the d2vision diagram spec both renderings come from, written without the Markdown stamp so it stays valid JSON. The problem tree guide explains each part.

docs.title: Effects
docs.text:
effects:
  - id: eff-diabetes
    statement: Diabetes and heart disease
  - id: eff-costs
    statement: Higher health costs
    parents: [eff-diabetes]
outcomes:
  - id: oc-eat-well
    title: People eat well
    level: impact
    addressesEffects: [eff-diabetes]

An effect has a statement, the effects it follows from, affected groups, evidence, an optional out-of-scope reason, and provenance. Validation reports an effect without a statement (VAL-EFF-001), one among its own parents (VAL-EFF-002), a chain of parents that loops (VAL-EFF-003), and one set aside without a reason (VAL-EFF-004). The effect element command adds and changes effects, and outcome set --relieves names the effects an outcome relieves.

docs.title: Causes as a network
docs.text: A cause's parents are the causes it contributes to, so structural causes feed underlying ones, underlying feed immediate, and immediate causes lead to the core problem. Validation now finds a loop through any branch of the network. Causes also take provenance, so one can be rejected in review like other elements.

docs.title: Lint
docs.text:
Three new rules, 72 in all:

  • IMP-EFF-001: each effect is relieved by an outcome or set aside with a reason
  • IMP-EFF-002: effects are relieved by long-term or impact outcomes, not only by earlier ones
  • IMP-CAU-003: a cause contributes only to causes at its own level or nearer the problem, which catches a link written the wrong way round

The cause rules now skip rejected causes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: The examples linked their causes the wrong way round, from the nearer cause to the deeper one, and now point from deeper causes toward the problem. In the membership network, working alone feeds both of the immediate causes. Both the membership network and the course catalog gain the effects of their core problems, each relieved by a long-term or impact outcome.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
• A new problem tree guide.
  • The authoring, CLI, examples, and getting started guides cover effects and the problem tree, and the README and concepts page list it as a projection.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
go install github.com/ProductBuildersHQ/impact-model/cmd/impact-model@v0.5.0

Go 1.26.5 or later. To draw the D2 diagram you also need the d2 tool.

docs.title: Documents: parent is now parents
docs.text:
A cause that names a parent must name it in a list. Validation refuses the old field:

error VAL-SCH-001 /causes/2: additional properties 'parent' not allowed

# was
causes:
  - id: cause-fast-food
    level: underlying
    parent: cause-busy

# is
causes:
  - id: cause-fast-food
    level: underlying
    parents:
      - cause-busy

In JSON, "parent": "cause-busy" becomes "parents": ["cause-busy"]. Nothing else in a document changes; specVersion stays "0.1".

While you are there, check which way the links point. A cause's parents are the causes it contributes to, nearer the problem. If an immediate cause names an underlying or structural one as its parent, the link is reversed, and IMP-CAU-003 now reports it.

docs.title: Command line
docs.text: cause add and cause set take --parents, which accepts several IDs, in place of --parent.

docs.title: Go code
docs.text: impact.Cause.Parent string is now Parents []string. Other changes are additions: impact.Effect, Model.Effects, Outcome.AddressesEffects, Cause.Provenance, and the problemtree package.

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text: An API comparison against v0.4.0 reports one incompatible change, the removal of Cause.Parent, and the additions above as compatible. The command line keeps its exit codes, and a model with no causes or effects is unaffected.

docs.title: Known Limitations
docs.text:
• Labels are not wrapped, so a long problem statement makes a wide box. Keep the core problem to a short phrase and put the detail in the narrative.
  • Row order is file order, so arrows between rows can cross; reorder causes or effects in the file to change it.
  • Mermaid places rows itself. Only the D2 rendering keeps every row in place.
  • The limitations of v0.4.0 still apply.

docs.title: Theory of Change: Research Brief
docs.text:
Purpose: background research to inform a Go-struct-first data model and JSON Schema for representing, measuring and reporting on Theories of Change (ToC).

Source access: the full texts of the ActKnowledge ToC Basics primer, the ActKnowledge Technical Papers, the ORS/Annie E. Casey guide (a mirrored PDF; the aecf.org page is behind a bot wall), the UNDG UNDAF companion guidance and Vogel's DFID review were all read. Other material was read through secondary sources, as noted in the citations.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The canonical sources broadly agree on the definition. They differ in emphasis:

  • ActKnowledge (Taplin & Clark, 2012): "a rigorous yet participatory process whereby groups and stakeholders in a planning process articulate their long-term goals and identify the conditions they believe have to unfold for those goals to be met. These conditions are modeled as desired outcomes, arranged graphically in a causal framework."
  • UNDG (2017): "a method that explains how a given intervention, or set of interventions, are expected to lead to a specific development change, drawing on a causal analysis based on available evidence."
  • Vogel / DFID (2012): "an outcomes-based approach which applies critical thinking to the design, implementation and evaluation of initiatives and programmes intended to support change in their contexts". Vogel treats a ToC as both a process and a product.
  • Rick Davies (quoted in Vogel): "The description of a sequence of events that is expected to lead to a particular desired outcome."

docs.title: Origins
docs.text:
• Program-theory evaluation, 1970s–80s. Chen, Rossi, Patton, Fitz-Gibbon and Weiss developed theory-driven evaluation. The Logical Framework (USAID, 1969) belongs to the same family.
  • Carol Weiss, 1995. In Nothing as Practical as Good Theory, published in the Aspen Roundtable volume New Approaches to Evaluating Comprehensive Community Initiatives (Connell, Kubisch, Schorr & Weiss, eds.), Weiss argued that complex initiatives are hard to evaluate because their assumptions are left implicit. She popularised the term "theory of change" and urged that the expected sequence of outcomes be mapped so evaluation could track it.
  • Aspen Institute Roundtable on Community Change. Kubisch (1997) set the three quality criteria: plausible, doable/feasible and testable. Andrea Anderson's The Community Builder's Approach to Theory of Change (2005) became the practical field guide.
  • ActKnowledge and the Center for Theory of Change. Hélène Clark and Dana Taplin formalised the method: backwards mapping, preconditions, rationales, the accountability ceiling, and indicator components. They released the TOCO software (theoryofchange.org, from 2002) and founded the Center for Theory of Change (2013).
  • Spread through international development in the 2010s. Uptake was driven by Comic Relief (James, 2011), DFID (Vogel, 2012), the Asia Foundation (Stein & Valters, 2012), UNICEF (Rogers, 2014) and UNDG (2017). ToC is now standard among foundations (Casey, Kellogg, Rockefeller, Ford), multilaterals and research funders.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Sources consistently name five purposes:

  • Planning and design: reach agreement on what has to change, in what order.
  • Filling the "missing middle": explain how activities connect to long-term goals.
  • Evaluability: a basis for indicators and for testing assumptions.
  • Communication and alignment: across partners, funders and staff.
  • Learning and adaptive management: "a living framework," revised as evidence arrives.

ORS describes the ToC as a "companion to action" and lists its uses as planning, accountability, resource allocation, communication and direction of action.

docs.title: 2. Core concepts and vocabulary
docs.text:
The definitions below follow the canonical sources. Where the sources differ, the difference is noted.

Concept Definition (source) Problem statement The core issue the group is addressing, bounded by where and for whom. The long-term outcome is its "positive opposite" (ActKnowledge). Ultimate goal / Impact A vision "beyond, or grander, than they can achieve through the initiative." It sits above the accountability ceiling (ActKnowledge). In RBM/OECD usage, "impact" means higher-level, long-term effects, positive or negative, intended or unintended. Long-term outcome (LTO) / Long-term goal "The goal you want to reach which is the purpose of your program." Every other outcome is a precondition to it (ActKnowledge). Outcome "A state, or condition, that must exist for your initiative to work and does not currently exist." It may be a change in people, organizations or places, and is phrased as a positive condition, not an activity (ActKnowledge). Short-term / intermediate / long-term outcomes Positions along the pathway. ORS attaches time horizons (e.g. 1–3 years and more than 3 years). UNDG uses levels of causality: immediate, underlying, structural/root. Precondition Any outcome other than the LTO: "conditions that must exist in order for the next outcome in the pathway to be achieved." Preconditions should be necessary and collectively sufficient (Technical Papers). Pathway of change / Outcomes framework "The sequence outcomes must occur in order to reach your long-term goal." It is drawn as chains from early outcomes (bottom) to the LTO (top). Most initiatives have several pathways. The full map is the "outcomes framework." Cluster A group of preconditions that together act as a joint precondition, with internal links left undrawn (ActKnowledge). In effect this is an AND-group. Causal link (connector/arrow) A claim that outcome A, possibly together with others, enables outcome B. UNDG notes that links can run horizontally as well as vertically. Rationale / Justification "Statements about why we expect one set of outcomes to lead to another". They explain each causal link and are often grounded in research or experience. Assumption ActKnowledge: "conditions or resources… needed for the success of your program, and which you believe already exist and will not be problematic to maintain." This contrasts with preconditions, which must be brought about. UNDG: "things taken for granted," stated as if X, then Y, because Z. Assumption types UNDG: causality, implementation, external factors, partnerships. theoryofchange.org: links between outcome levels, completeness of preconditions, justification of intervention-to-outcome links, and context. ORS: philosophies, principles or values, ways of working together, and community context. Mayne's COM-B model: assumptions on reach, capacity change, behaviour change, direct benefits and wellbeing. Intervention "The things your program or group of stakeholders will undertake to bring about outcomes." Strategy = "a coordinated sequence of interventions." Activity = the specific actions within an intervention. ActKnowledge places interventions on the connector between precondition and outcome. One intervention may serve many outcomes. Output In RBM and logframes, the direct products or services delivered by activities (within management control). ActKnowledge folds outputs into interventions ("activities and outputs of any sort"). Indicator "Measurable evidence of meeting a goal". It may be quantitative or qualitative. Each indicator has four components: population (who or what changes), target (how many), threshold (how much change is "good enough") and timeline (by when). Formula: "How many of who or what will reach what level by when?" Baseline "A measure of population for any indicators at the outset of the initiative, used for comparison" (ActKnowledge glossary). Ceiling of accountability A dashed line drawn above the LTO. Outcomes below it are ones the group holds itself accountable for. Goals above it are shown for vision and communication but not claimed. Narrative A one-to-two-page summary that explains the pathways and highlights key assumptions, rationales and interventions. Risk Factors that could stop change from happening as assumed. UNDG: "assumptions and risks are often inversely related". UNDG risk types: environmental/political, opportunities, design, partnerships. External factors / context Conditions outside the initiative's work that help or hinder change (Vogel: "social, political and environmental conditions… other actors able to influence change"). Stakeholders / actors / partners UNDG step 4: the actors "likely to have a direct role in determining the success or failure," the partners and who does what. The solution tree may show changes delivered by others that are still monitored. Boundary partners From Outcome Mapping (IDRC): the actors a program works with directly and hopes to influence but does not control. Change is expressed as outcome challenges and graded progress markers ("expect / like / love to see"). Spheres of control / influence / interest RBM and Outcome Mapping framing. Control covers inputs, activities and outputs. Influence covers behaviour change among direct partners. Interest covers state or wellbeing change. This maps closely onto the accountability ceiling. Problem tree / solution tree UNDG: immediate, underlying and structural root causes are mapped into a problem tree and then converted into a solution tree. The solution tree is the skeleton of the ToC and need not mirror the problem tree exactly. Outcome categories (ORS/Casey) Impact: changes in the conditions of people (knowledge, attitudes, skills, behaviour, health, financial status) and population-level conditions. Influence: changes in "policies, regulations, systems, practice or public opinion," including visibility of an issue, norms, partnerships, public will, service practice and business practice. Leverage: changes in investment by other funders. Underneath these sit core capacities: governance, data use, partnerships and similar. "So that" chains (ORS) Forward reasoning: Strategy → so that → outcome → so that → outcome…, with each step tagged by category. This complements backwards mapping. Scope Narrow or broad (how many pathways) crossed with shallow or deep (how many precondition levels), giving four types (Technical Papers / Clark 2004).

docs.title: 3. Process for constructing a ToC, and what each step produces
ActKnowledge six-stage method
docs.text: # Step Artifact produced 0 Elicit and bound the problem statement Problem statement (where, for whom) 1 Identify the long-term goal or LTO; optionally an ultimate goal above the ceiling LTO definition (agreed terms, e.g. what "safe" means); accountability ceiling 2 Backwards mapping: "What preconditions must exist?" Repeat down to the earliest changes; test whether each set is necessary and sufficient Outcomes framework: a graph of outcomes and causal links, pathways, clusters 3 Surface assumptions; write rationales for the links Assumption list; rationale per link 4 Identify interventions; place them on connectors; map existing programs; flag gaps Intervention-to-link mapping; gap list 5 Develop indicators (population, target, threshold, timeline) for every outcome, or at least every intervention-targeted outcome Indicator set / measurement framework 6 Quality review (plausible, feasible, testable) and narrative QA record; 1–2 page narrative

docs.title: UNDG four steps (validated against evidence at each step)
docs.text:
1. Focus: high-level change, prioritised by equity, comparative advantage and feasibility.
  2. Change analysis: problem tree to solution tree; immediate, underlying and structural causes; what partners already contribute.
  3. Assumptions and risks: for each assumption, ask three questions. Does it fully explain the change? Is it plausible given the evidence? Does it need testing?
  4. Partners and actors: who does what; elements vital to success but outside the program, which are still monitored.

The UNDG guidance also includes a quality checklist. It requires that M&E provisions name the assumptions that need testing and that evaluation assess "the validity of the theory of change."

docs.title: ORS/Casey
docs.text: ORS produces two products, an outcome map and a list of assumptions. It adds "so that" chains, categorisation of outcomes as impact, influence or leverage, prioritisation (develop detailed ToCs for strategies expected to show change in 1–3 years), and non-linear representations (web, starburst, organism).

docs.title: Implications for a tool
docs.text:
• The workflow is staged.
  • Partial ToCs are legitimate states (e.g. outcomes without interventions yet).
  • Indicators are sometimes defined during mapping to settle what an ambiguous outcome means.

docs.title: Indicators and the measurement framework
docs.text:
Each outcome should have at least one indicator. In practice, a prioritised subset is put into operation, based on data availability, persuasiveness and whether the indicator can stand in for other outcomes. Standard RBM and M&E plan fields per indicator:

  • definition and unit
  • direction of desired change
  • baseline (value, date, source)
  • target(s) and threshold
  • milestones (interim targets)
  • means or source of verification
  • collection method
  • frequency
  • responsible party
  • disaggregation (sex, geography, segment)

SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable/Attributable, Relevant, Time-bound) is the usual indicator quality test. Outcome Mapping's progress markers are a graduated alternative for behavioural change: "expect / like / love to see." They are read as a set, not one at a time.

docs.title: Timeline consistency
docs.text: ActKnowledge notes that an outcome's timeline depends on the outcomes above and below it. A downstream target cannot be earlier than its upstream precondition. This is a constraint a validator can check.

docs.title: Attribution versus contribution
docs.text:
In complex settings, population-level change can rarely be attributed to a single actor. ToC-based evaluation therefore uses contribution claims.

Contribution Analysis (Mayne 2001, 2008, 2012) has six iterative steps:

  1. Set out the cause-effect (attribution or contribution) question.
  2. Develop the ToC and the risks to it.
  3. Gather existing evidence on the ToC.
  4. Assemble and assess the contribution story and the challenges to it.
  5. Seek additional evidence.
  6. Revise and strengthen the contribution story, looping back to step 4.

A contribution claim is credible when four conditions hold: the ToC is plausible, it was implemented as intended, the expected chain of results occurred and the assumptions held (a verified ToC), and other influencing factors were assessed and accounted for. Mayne's later robust ToC / COM-B work structures each link as reach → capacity change (capability, opportunity, motivation) → behaviour change → direct benefits → wellbeing, with a separate assumption set for each link and explicit external influences.

docs.title: Evidence strength
docs.text:
Process tracing, often combined with Contribution Analysis (Befani & Mayne, 2014), grades evidence for a causal link using four tests:

Test Necessary? Sufficient? Straw-in-the-wind no no Hoop yes no Smoking gun no yes Doubly decisive yes yes

Bayesian updating approaches (Befani & Stedman-Bryce) turn these into confidence levels. A simpler ordinal scale (strong / moderate / weak / none / contradicting) is common in practice. Evidence sources include research literature, prior evaluation, monitoring data, expert judgement and stakeholder testimony.

docs.title: Assumption testing
docs.text: UNDG's three questions mark each assumption as plausible or not and as needing testing or not. During implementation, assumptions should be monitored, sometimes with their own indicators, and assigned a status: holding, weakening, or failed.

docs.title: Complementary methods
docs.text:
• Outcome Harvesting (Wilson-Grau & Britt, 2012) works backwards from observed change. It collects outcome statements (what changed, for whom, when, where), notes the significance of each and the contribution of the intervention, substantiates them with independent informants, and compares them to the ToC to find unanticipated pathways. It has six steps: design, gather data and draft outcome descriptions, engage informants, substantiate, analyse and interpret, and support use.
  • Most Significant Change (Davies & Dart, 2005) collects stories of change within domains of change, then selects the most significant through structured stakeholder panels that record their reasons for choosing. It is qualitative and participatory, and useful for spotting unexpected outcomes and value shifts.
  • OECD-DAC criteria (revised 2019): relevance, coherence, effectiveness, efficiency, impact, sustainability. Evaluations of a ToC-based program typically report against these.

docs.title: Adaptive management and revision
docs.text: All sources stress that a ToC is a living model. Monitoring data feeds back into the theory: pathways are revised, assumptions retested, interventions dropped. Patrizi warned against treating the ToC as a fixed plan, and Vogel recommended performance management that "tolerates uncertainty." Every revision should therefore be versioned, with the reason for change, the evidence that triggered it, and a diff.

docs.title: 5. Common artifacts and deliverables
docs.text:
1. Pathway diagram / outcomes framework map: boxes and arrows, with the ceiling line, intervention symbols on connectors, and clusters. There are usually two versions: a detailed working map and a simplified communication map.
  2. Narrative: 1–2 pages.
  3. Assumptions table: assumption, type, linked element, evidence, plausibility, whether testing is needed, status, linked risk.
  4. Risk register: risk, category, likelihood, impact, mitigation, linked assumption.
  5. Indicator / measurement framework (results framework, M&E plan): one row per indicator, with baseline, targets, milestones, source, frequency and owner.
  6. Logframe (often derived from the ToC for donors): a 4×4 matrix. Rows are goal, purpose/outcome, outputs and activities. Columns are narrative summary, objectively verifiable indicators, means of verification and assumptions.
  7. Actor / partner map: roles, boundary partners, division of labour.
  8. Problem tree and solution tree.
  9. Progress reports and dashboards: indicator actual against target, outcome status rolled up by pathway, assumption health, and contribution narrative. These go to leadership, funders or a public audience. ISEAL and DCED require public or audited reporting.
  10. Evaluation reports: a contribution story, validity of the ToC, and recommended revisions.

docs.title: 6. ToC compared with logic model, logframe and results chain
docs.text:
Theory of Change Logic model Logframe (LFA) Results chain Core form Causal network of outcomes, with rationales, assumptions and interventions Linear columns: inputs → activities → outputs → outcomes → impact (Kellogg, 2004) 4×4 matrix with an assumptions column (USAID, 1969) Linear chain of the same five levels (RBM, DCED) Direction of reasoning Backwards from the goal Forwards ("if… then") Top-down hierarchy Forwards Explains why links hold Yes (rationales, evidence) Rarely Only through the assumptions column Rarely Multiple pathways, non-linearity Yes Limited No Limited (DCED allows branches) Context and other actors Explicit Usually absent External assumptions only Sometimes Main use Strategy, learning, evaluation design Program description and communication Contracting, accountability, monitoring Results measurement, attribution

A recurring point in the sources: "a logic model without reference to the context [is] more of a log-frame than a theory of change" (Vogel). Logic models and logframes can be generated from a ToC by flattening it, but not the reverse. For a data model, this means the ToC graph should be the primary structure, with logframe and logic-model views produced by projection.

docs.title: Critiques that matter for modelling
docs.text:
• Rick Davies (2018), "Representing Theories of Change": most ToC diagrams are technically poor. They give too much attention to the arrows and too little to the events (nodes), leave AND/OR relationships ambiguous, cannot be evaluated, and ignore feedback. Davies argues for network representations and software. He also distinguishes temporal ToCs (sequenced) from atemporal ones (configurational).
  • Linearity critiques (complexity scholars): real change involves feedback loops and emergence. A ToC models belief, not reality.
  • "ToC-washing": logframes or strategic plans relabelled as ToCs. Terms such as output, outcome and impact are used inconsistently.

The design response is explicit node semantics, explicit gate logic, optional cycles and evaluability validation.

docs.title: 7. Applicability to business, market and technology-ecosystem change
docs.text:
The literature on ToC outside the nonprofit and development sector is thinner but directly relevant:

  • Market Systems Development (MSD / M4P). Practical Action's PMSD toolkit defines a ToC as linking "project activities, market actor behaviour changes, market system changes and impacts on target groups." The Adopt–Adapt–Expand–Respond (AAER) framework (Springfield Centre; Nippard, Hitchins & Elliott, 2014) models systemic change among competing market actors:
    • Adopt: pilot partners take up a practice and benefit from it.
    • Adapt: they invest independently and continue without support.
    • Expand: competitors copy or crowd in.
    • Respond: non-competing supporting actors (regulators, service providers) adjust.

This maps almost exactly onto driving adoption of a technical standard. A Uganda case found adoption stalled because of weak competition, which forced a ToC revision: an assumption about market structure had failed. - DCED Standard for Results Measurement (private-sector development). It covers results chains, indicators for each key change, attribution estimation, systemic-change measurement, cost tracking and audit. It is structured as control points with must and recommended levels, a useful precedent for conformance levels in a spec. - Voluntary sustainability standards (ISEAL Code, 2024; formerly Impacts Code v2.0). Standards bodies must define intended impacts, publish a ToC, keep it current through defined procedures, and run M&E with feedback loops and public reporting. Rainforest Alliance publishes its ToC as outcomes, strategies (causal pathways) and indicators. This is the clearest real-world case of a ToC for driving adoption of a standard across a market. - Collective Impact (Kania & Kramer, SSIR 2011). Here several organisations, including competitors, share a common agenda, shared measurement, mutually reinforcing activities, continuous communication and a backbone organisation. The data model needs multi-actor ownership of outcomes and shared indicators. - Industry transition research. Studies describe green-practice transitions moving through initiation, then adoption via voluntary standards, then legitimation through framing, then commercialisation by new entrants. Contribution comes from several stakeholders, not a single leader. - Corporate strategy analogues. These are not labelled ToC but share its structure: - Kaplan & Norton strategy maps (cause-effect links across balanced-scorecard perspectives) - Rumelt's diagnosis, guiding policy and coherent actions - "working backwards" product planning - OKRs (outcome-level objectives with key-result indicators) - Rogers' diffusion of innovations (adoption-curve segments as populations for indicators) - Philanthropy and impact investing. Brest (2010) and Jackson (2013) apply ToC to investment portfolios, where additionality is the counterpart of contribution.

docs.title: Implications for a market or ecosystem ToC
docs.text:
• Actors can be competitors, with incentive-based assumptions such as "first-movers gain advantage."
  • Outcomes are commonly behaviour or practice changes by organisations, the Influence category, rather than changes in individual wellbeing.
  • Indicators are often adoption counts or shares within a defined population (the market segment).
  • Network effects and tipping points introduce reinforcing feedback loops and threshold (k-of-n) logic.
  • Accountability sits at "influence." Market-wide impact is above the ceiling.

docs.title: 8.1 Entities
docs.text:
Entities are marked [C] for core and [E] for optional or extension. Cardinalities are given in parentheses.

ImpactModel [C] is the root document.

  • Fields: id, name, version, status (draft / active / under_review / archived), scope {breadth, depth}, timeHorizon, problemStatement, narrative, owners[], createdAt, updatedAt.
  • Contains (1:N): outcomes, links, preconditionGroups, interventions, assumptions, indicators, evidence, risks, actors, externalFactors, revisions.
  • accountabilityCeiling: the ID(s) of the highest accountable outcome(s), or a level marker.

Outcome [C] is a node.

  • Fields: id, statement (a positive condition, not an activity), description, level (enum: impact / long_term / intermediate / short_term), category [E] (impact / influence / leverage / capacity; or COM-B reach / capability / opportunity / motivation / behavior / direct_benefit / wellbeing), changeType [E] (knowledge / attitude / skill / behavior / practice / policy / norm / condition / investment / adoption).
  • accountability (enum: accountable / contributory / above_ceiling).
  • sphere [E] (control / influence / interest).
  • population (who or what changes), timeframe, pathwayIds[], clusterId?, priority, ownerActorIds[] (N:M, which supports shared or collective outcomes).
  • status is derived (see 8.3).

CausalLink [C] is a directed edge from a source node to a target node.

  • Fields: id, from (an Outcome, or an Intervention for the activity-to-outcome links in logic-model style), to (an Outcome or a PreconditionGroup).
  • rationale (text), assumptionIds[] (N:M), evidenceIds[] (N:M), confidence / evidenceStrength (enum: strong / moderate / weak / none / contested).
  • polarity [E] (positive / negative), lag [E] (duration), isFeedback [E] (bool), loopType [E] (reinforcing / balancing).
  • interventionIds[]: ActKnowledge places interventions on connectors.

PreconditionGroup [C] carries the AND/OR semantics; ActKnowledge calls this a "cluster."

  • Fields: id, targetOutcomeId, memberOutcomeIds[] (≥ 2), logic (enum: all [AND, the default necessary-and-sufficient set] / any [OR, alternative pathways] / threshold with minCount [k-of-n] / weighted [E]).
  • sufficiencyAssessment (text or enum).
  • Groups may nest (a member may be another group), which allows expressions such as (A AND B) OR C.

Pathway [E] is a named subset of nodes and edges (e.g. "law-enforcement pathway"), for views and reporting rollups.

Intervention [C] covers strategies, programs and initiatives.

  • Fields: id, name, type (enum: strategy / intervention / activity, hierarchical through parentId), description, targets (links or outcomes it is meant to produce, 1:N), ownerActorIds[], status (planned / active / paused / completed / discontinued), startDate, endDate, resources / budget [E], outputs[] [E] (deliverables with output indicators).
  • category [E]: ORS impact / influence / leverage approach, or MSD AAER stage targeted.

Assumption [C]

  • Fields: id, statement (preferably if X then Y because Z), type (enum: causal / contextual / implementation / partnership / completeness / values), appliesTo (polymorphic refs to links, outcomes, interventions or the whole ToC; N:M).
  • plausibility (high / medium / low), criticality (high / medium / low), needsTesting (bool), testMethod, status (enum: untested / holding / weakening / failed / revised), evidenceIds[], indicatorIds[] (assumption-monitoring indicators), relatedRiskIds[].

Risk [E, recommended]

  • Fields: id, description, category (political_environmental / design / partnership / market / technical / operational / opportunity), likelihood, impact, mitigation, ownerActorId, relatedAssumptionIds[], status.

ExternalFactor [E]: contextual conditions or other actors' work that affect outcomes.

  • Fields: id, description, effect (enabling / hindering), affects[] (refs), monitored (bool).

Actor [C-lite] covers stakeholders, partners and competitors.

  • Fields: id, name, type (organization / group / individual / segment), roles[] (enum: owner / implementer / partner / funder / boundary_partner / beneficiary / target_adopter / competitor / regulator / influencer / backbone), relationship (control / influence / interest).
  • Referenced by outcomes (who changes), interventions (who acts) and indicators (population).

Indicator [C]

  • Fields: id, name, measures (an Outcome, Intervention/output or Assumption; N:1 per indicator), definition, type (quantitative / qualitative / binary / milestone / progress_marker), unit, direction (increase / decrease / maintain / achieve).
  • The four ActKnowledge components:
    • population {description, actorIds or segment, size}
    • target {count or proportion of the population}
    • threshold {level of change considered sufficient}
    • timeline {due date}
  • baseline {value, date, sourceId, notes}, targets[] {value, dueDate, threshold, label}, milestones[] (interim targets).
  • dataSource, collectionMethod, frequency (enum or ISO-8601 duration), responsibleActorId, disaggregations[].
  • smartCheck [E], proxyFor[] [E] (outcome IDs this indicator stands in for), progressMarkerLevel [E] (expect / like / love).

Measurement (Observation) [C]: time-series data points.

  • Fields: id, indicatorId, value (number / string / bool), periodStart, periodEnd (or observedAt), disaggregation {key: value}, sourceId, dataQuality (verified / reported / estimated), notes, recordedBy.

Evidence [E, recommended]

  • Fields: id, type (research / evaluation / monitoring_data / expert_judgment / stakeholder_testimony / case_study / outcome_harvest / msc_story), citation / url, summary, strength (strong / moderate / weak), processTracingTest [E] (straw_in_the_wind / hoop / smoking_gun / doubly_decisive), supports / contradicts (refs), date.

ContributionClaim [E]: Contribution Analysis output.

  • Fields: id, outcomeId, interventionIds[], claim, rivalExplanations[] (external factors), evidenceIds[], confidence, conditions {plausible, implementedAsIntended, chainObserved, otherFactorsAccounted} (bools), assessedAt.

ObservedOutcome [E]: Outcome Harvesting and MSC records of actual, possibly unanticipated, change.

  • Fields: id, description, actorId, when, where, significance, contribution, substantiated (bool), mappedOutcomeId? (null means unanticipated, which suggests a revision to the ToC).

Review / Revision [C for versioning]

  • Fields: id, version, date, type (quality_review / periodic_review / evaluation / adaptive_change), qualityCriteria {plausible, feasible, testable: pass / partial / fail + notes}, changes[] (added / removed / modified element refs), rationale, triggerEvidenceIds[], decisions[].

Report / Snapshot [E]: generated, not stored as source data.

  • Fields: asOf, audience (leadership / funder / public / partners), status rollups, indicator actual against target, assumption health, risks, contribution narrative. Logframe and logic-model views are projections from the graph.

ProblemTree [E]: Cause nodes {id, statement, level (immediate / underlying / structural), parentId}, plus a mapping from causes to the solution outcomes that address them.

docs.title: 8.2 Graph semantics
docs.text:
• Nodes are typed: outcome (with level), intervention, assumption, external factor, risk. Only outcomes and interventions take part in the causal backbone. Assumptions, risks and external factors attach to links or nodes as annotations.
  • Edges are directed CausalLinks meaning "contributes to / is a precondition of." The default reading of all incoming edges to a node is AND: preconditions are jointly necessary. Any other logic must be stated explicitly through a PreconditionGroup (OR, k-of-n, nested), which addresses Davies's ambiguity critique. A validator should warn when a node has more than one incoming edge with no stated logic, if the spec chooses to require explicitness.
  • Acyclicity: the backbone, excluding links marked isFeedback: true, should be a DAG. Feedback links (reinforcing / balancing) are allowed but must be declared. This supports network effects and adoption tipping points.
  • Root and leaves: exactly one (or a declared small set of) LTOs at the accountability ceiling. Optional impact nodes sit above the ceiling. Every outcome should have a path to an LTO; orphans are a validation warning.
  • Level monotonicity: edges should go from lower or equal levels to higher levels (short-term to intermediate to long-term to impact). Same-level horizontal links are allowed, as UNDG notes.
  • Interventions attach either to a link (ActKnowledge style, "what it takes for A to produce B") or directly to an outcome. Both should be supported, with a mode flag.
  • Timeline consistency: an outcome's indicator due date should be no earlier than the due dates of its preconditions. This is checkable.
  • Ceiling semantics: an outcome above the ceiling must not be accountable. Contribution claims apply above the ceiling and attribution or achievement claims below it.

docs.title: 8.3 Measurement semantics
docs.text:
• Indicator status is computed from the latest measurement against the applicable milestone or target: no_data / not_started / on_track / at_risk / off_track / achieved / missed. Direction-aware comparison and threshold logic handle increase, decrease and maintain.
  • Outcome status is derived, never set directly. It rolls up from the outcome's indicators using a stated aggregation (all / any / weighted / primary-indicator). Optionally it is gated by precondition-group logic: an outcome cannot be "achieved" while required preconditions are off-track, unless there is an explicit override with a reason. This mirrors the convention that a roadmap phase status is derived from its items.
  • Pathway and ToC health roll up outcome statuses, assumption statuses (count of failed or weakening critical assumptions) and risks.
  • Revision triggers: a failed assumption, a missed milestone on a critical link, or an unanticipated ObservedOutcome should create a review prompt. This is the adaptive-management loop.
  • Provenance: every measurement and evidence item cites a source. Reports state the as-of date and the data quality.

docs.title: 8.4 Core and extension summary
docs.text:
Core (minimum viable ToC, matching Vogel's consensus elements and the ActKnowledge components):

  • ImpactModel (problem statement, narrative, ceiling)
  • Outcome
  • CausalLink (with rationale)
  • PreconditionGroup (AND/OR)
  • Intervention
  • Assumption
  • Indicator (population / target / threshold / timeline, baseline, targets)
  • Measurement
  • Actor (minimal)
  • Revision

Extension modules:

  • Risk and ExternalFactor
  • Evidence and process-tracing grades
  • ContributionClaim
  • ObservedOutcome (Outcome Harvesting / MSC)
  • ProblemTree
  • Pathway views
  • Outcome category taxonomies (ORS impact/influence/leverage, COM-B, MSD AAER, ISEAL)
  • Feedback loops
  • Outputs and budgets
  • Logframe and logic-model projections
  • Reports and dashboards

Taxonomies should be pluggable as extensible enumerations so that development, corporate and market-adoption ToCs can share one core.

docs.title: 9. Primary-source review: UNDG UNDAF Companion Guidance (2017)
docs.text: A full read of the 15-page UNDG guidance. It confirms the summaries above: the four steps, the three assumption questions, the assumption and risk types, and the cause levels. It also adds the details below, which matter for the data model. Page numbers refer to the PDF.

docs.title: 9.1 Principles and structure
docs.text:
• Three principles (p. 5). A ToC is:
    • developed consultatively;
    • grounded in, tested with, and revised on evidence at all stages;
    • a support for continuous learning from design to closure.
  • Validation at every step (p. 5). Each of the four steps (focus, change analysis, assumptions and risks, partners and actors) is validated against evidence and through stakeholder consultation. This is drawn as a loop around the steps, not as a final gate.
  • Nested theories (pp. 4, 13). An overarching ToC is supported by:
    • outcome-level ToCs that explain the outputs in each results group's work plan;
    • optionally, agency-specific ToCs.

All are linked to the overarching ToC and kept as annexes that are re-validated during monitoring.

docs.title: 9.2 Step 1 — Focus (p. 6)
docs.text:
High-level changes are selected against explicit criteria:

  • Equity: leaving no one behind, and gender equality.
  • Comparative advantage: the mandate and ability to build lasting capacity; where the organization can have the greatest impact.
  • Feasibility.

docs.title: 9.3 Step 2 — Change analysis (pp. 6–8)
docs.text:
• Problem tree. Start from a problem tree with immediate, underlying, and structural/root causes. Branches are organized into pathways that link cause levels and show how they interlink.
  • Solution tree. Convert the problem tree into a solution tree with an expected solution for each level of causality. The solution tree need not mirror the problem tree, but every cause must be addressed. Capacity-development needs appear at the underlying level.
  • Criteria for solutions. Proposed solutions are checked against equity, comparative advantage, feasibility (resources, partnerships, political, cultural, or operational risks), and what works: evidence of the scale of change achieved by similar solutions, and of where they failed.
  • Partner-delivered parts are still monitored. The solution tree includes changes that other partners deliver. The organization prioritizes a subset (Figure 3 colours the prioritized boxes differently), but "will still monitor progress of the entire solution tree … because failure to achieve results in an area where other partners work will most likely hinder the achievement of the ultimate objective."
  • Horizontal links. Cause–effect links may run horizontally as well as vertically.
  • Equity review before Step 3. The ToC must:
    • target the most vulnerable;
    • address inequality and its root causes, not only immediate ones;
    • explicitly target women and girls;
    • aim at sustainable change through institutions.

docs.title: 9.4 Step 3 — Assumptions and risks (pp. 8–9)
docs.text:
Assumptions. These are written as if X, then Y, because Z and assessed against evidence. There are four types:

  • Causality: the mechanism by which one result leads to another.
  • Implementation: design and targeting of the interventions.
  • External factors: influences from outside the area of work.
  • Partnerships: conflicts among partners' interests; the ability to take on new partners.

Each assumption gets three questions:

  1. Does it fully explain the change? If not, refine it or add assumptions.
  2. Is it plausible, given the evidence and stakeholders' experience?
  3. Does it need testing, through evaluation or close monitoring?

Risks. Exploring assumptions first helps surface risks, because the two are "often inversely related". There are four categories:

  • Environmental and political: elections, staff turnover in government, disasters, policy changes, commodity prices.
  • Opportunities: whether the organization can take advantage of future opportunities.
  • Design: targeting difficulties, missing data or access, rigidity.
  • Partnerships.

Only the most important risks need isolating. When they materialize, assumptions are revised and the ToC adapted.

docs.title: 9.5 Step 4 — Partners and key actors (p. 9)
docs.text:
• Division of labour. For each result: who does what, where two or more entities must collaborate, and how to avoid overlap.
  • Elements outside the organization's reach. Some elements are vital to success but outside what the organization can address directly. They may not appear in the results framework, but they are recognized as factors and may be pursued through advocacy or other engagement strategies.

docs.title: 9.6 Quality assurance checklist (p. 11)
docs.text:
The PDF lists the first two items twice, so there are 15 entries but 13 distinct items. Grouped for modelling:

Group Checklist items Generic? Process Collaborative, participatory process with multiple stakeholder perspectives, including marginalized voices Yes Logic Plausible, clear, logical flow "without any leaps of faith or gaps in logic"; root and underlying causes tackled, not just immediate ones Yes Assumptions and risks Clearly states the assumptions and risks most relevant to whether change will happen Yes Actors Identifies who does what, and the key partners whose effort is required Yes Evidence Refers to evidence from credible sources; identifies limitations in the evidence base to inform evaluation priorities Yes Equity and targeting Benefits the most vulnerable; targets women and girls; names specific changes for targeted groups "rather than relying on assumptions about how particular groups benefit" Partly. Targeted groups and disaggregation are generic; gender targeting is UN-specific Sustainability and resilience Strengthens institutions; resilience to shocks (climate, epidemics, hazards, conflict); poverty–environment links; structural causes of violence UN / development-specific Presentation A diagram embedded in the narrative of programme documents Yes

docs.title: 9.7 From ToC to programme document (p. 12)
docs.text:
The guidance maps ToC elements onto sections of the programme document:

  • Narrative summary: causal factors, how affected groups differ, and evidence.
  • Risks and assumptions: why these priorities were chosen; comparative advantage; risks with mitigation.
  • Initiatives outside the results matrix: partner-delivered parts of the solution tree.
  • Implementation arrangements: who does what.
  • M&E provisions: assumptions needing testing; regular monitoring and updating of the ToC; evaluation of the ToC's validity.
  • Communication of results.
  • Results matrix: outcomes tied to the high-level changes; indicators that measure the changes for targeted groups.

docs.title: 9.8 Implications for the data model
docs.text:
• Promote the problem tree (causes with levels, plus outcome-to-cause links) from extension to core-lite.
  • Add an outcome's responsibility (own, shared, partner, unaddressed) and its delivering actors. Monitoring covers all of these, while accountability covers only own and shared.
  • Generalize prioritization criteria to apply to outcomes and interventions (focus and solution selection), not only metrics.
  • Add the partnership assumption type. Add plausibility, needsTesting, and an optional structured if / then / because statement.
  • Give risks a category and related assumptions.
  • Record consultations / validations for each step: method, stakeholder groups, findings.
  • Declare target groups, and check that indicators disaggregate by them.
  • Make the QA checklist a rubric profile: generic items in the core rubric, development-sector items in an optional profile.
  • Add a narrative / programme-document report following §9.7, and a division-of-labour report following §9.5.

docs.title: PLAN — Theory of Change Specification — Go-first model, JSON Schema, measurement, and leadership reporting
docs.text:
Initiative: INIT-THEORYOFCHANGESPEC-001 Repository: github.com/ProductBuildersHQ/impact-model Version: 0.4 Status: Draft — pending tech-lead review (pbhq-lite gate: after PLAN)

This PLAN is non-normative. It sequences the work in PRD.md and TRD.md and must not add requirements. Execution state lives in ROADMAP.md.

docs.title: 1. Approach
docs.text:
Thin slice first, then deepen. The first five phases build one complete path from end to end:

minimal model → validate → edit → pathways, metric library, provenance → diagram, logic models, metric definitions, glossary, workshop deck, draft from public sources → assessment, review packet and sheet, review import, approval

That path is the first adopter milestone: draft a theory from public information, share it as familiar documents, take the organization's responses back in, and approve the agreed baseline. Later phases add depth behind interfaces the slice has already proven.

Why this order:

  1. Model, schema, load, validate, edit. Every consumer binds to the model. Every mutation goes through one validated patch engine from day one.
  2. Pathways, metric library, glossary, and provenance are the smallest additions a real organization needs. Provenance has to arrive with the first draft, because the first draft is typically built from public sources and every element must say whether it was stated or inferred.
  3. Workshop pack and source drafting. Diagram, logic models, metric definitions, glossary, CSV, a Marp workshop deck, and the draft-from-sources skill. Together they turn public sources into a presentable hypothesis theory.
  4. Review and agreement. The assessment report, the pandoc sharing profile with export stamps, the review packet and review sheet, review import as proposals, and approval. This closes the loop with people who never touch the tools. The loop is file-based, so it works with manual upload and download before any Google automation exists.
  5. Measurement-framework design. Metric selection and burden, stories, and UNDG change analysis.
  6. Quality. Lint profiles, the rubric, and judging.
  7. Measurement.
  8. Reporting, story, and presentations.
  9. Agents and revisions. The MCP server, skills, theory diff, and Google sharing automation. Google sharing waits on gogoogle and mcp-google (INIT-GOGOOGLE-001, INIT-MCPGOOGLE-001).
  10. Ecosystem integration and release.

Major bets:

  • The ToC graph is primary.
  • ObservationSet is a separate document.
  • Shared metric definitions plus deterministic tools.
  • All edits go through validated patches.
  • Decks reuse the report view.
  • Judging is file-based.
  • Provenance lives on every element.
  • Review responses are a channel-neutral file (ReviewResponse) imported as proposals. Google Drive is one channel, reached through external tooling; this module stays free of cloud dependencies.

Deliberately deferred:

  • contribution claims
  • substantiated observed outcomes
  • logframe matrices
  • XLSX
  • data connectors and record linkage
  • a hosted service
  • native PPTX generation in Go

docs.title: 1.1 Adopter milestones
docs.text:
The phases are ordered so a first adopter can use the tools at each stage of a ToC-based impact-measurement engagement. The adopter is a small-staff organization.
